1647	# The 0xSimao Method
1648	
1649	Derived from 869 published findings across 143 reviews. This is HOW to think. Your lens file is WHAT to look for. Work them together.
1650	
1651	## The core thesis
1652	
1653	Most auditors read code looking for bad lines. That finds the bugs a linter finds.
1654	
1655	0xSimao reads code looking for **a claim that has drifted from what actually backs it**. Value moves through a protocol in sequences: deposit, accrue, borrow, liquidate, withdraw. Each step writes some subset of the accounting state, and drift is any way that state stops describing reality:
1656	
1657	| Drift | Shape |
1658	| --- | --- |
1659	| The write is missing | value moved and no variable recorded it — or one branch updates it and the sibling branch does not |
1660	| The write is wrong | the variable is updated with the wrong amount, direction, rounding, units, or decimals |
1661	| The write is mistimed | the right value at the wrong moment, so someone's snapshot is taken against state that is about to change |
1662	| The write goes to the wrong party | the total is intact; the split between cohorts is not |
1663	| The input was never trustworthy | the number is faithfully propagated from an oracle, a live balance, or a caller-supplied parameter an attacker controls |
1664	| The state is unreachable | the accounting is correct but a revert, a pause, an unbounded loop, or a missing path means it can never be settled |
1665	
1666	The drift is invisible at any single line. It only appears when you ask: *after this whole sequence, does the protocol still owe exactly what it holds — and can everyone actually collect it?*
1667	
1668	A defect nobody can be shown to lose money from is a curiosity. So every candidate gets one more question, and it is the one that separates a finding from a smell:
1669	
1670	> **Who is left holding the loss?**
1671	
1672	Answer with a named class of actor, never "users". For accounting drift it is often whoever withdraws last, because a shortfall stays invisible until the balance runs out — but for a bricked liquidation it is the solvent lenders eating the bad debt, for a mistimed snapshot it is the cohort that held through the accrual, and for a forged signature it is whoever the forged message was drawn against. If the only person worse off is the caller, there is no finding.
1673	
1674	**This lens is the sharpest one, not the only one.** Accounting drift is the largest single class in his corpus, but it is not the majority of it. The rest is DoS and permanently stuck funds, access control and signature defects, token- and integration-behaviour assumptions (`USDT` approvals, fee-on-transfer, blacklists, pausable collateral), oracle and parameter validation, and cross-chain state — and those are what your lens file owns. Work the money map first because it is what makes the drift class visible; then work your lens on its own terms. When the target has little accounting to speak of — a router, a registry, a verifier, a signature scheme — say so, keep the money map short, and go straight to your lens. Do not force a finding into the drift frame to make it sound like his.
1675	
1676	## Phase 0 — Learn the protocol's own vocabulary before reading for bugs
1677	
1678	His findings are written in the protocol's language: `cdsPoolValue`, `abond`, `downsideProtected`, `unassignedEarnings`, `raBalance`, `floatingBackupBorrowed`. He does not audit "a vault"; he audits *this* vault's specific accounting model.
1679	
1680	Before hunting, be able to state in plain English:
1681	- What does a user give, and what claim do they receive in return?
1682	- What is that claim worth, and which variables determine the value?
1683	- Where does yield come from, and who is entitled to it?
1684	- What happens when the protocol is short — who absorbs the shortfall?
1685	
1686	If you cannot answer these without Solidity jargon, you are not ready to find his class of bug. Any spot where your plain-English explanation goes fuzzy is exactly where the bug is; mark it and come back.
1687	
1688	## Phase 1 — Build the money map
1689	
1690	For every storage variable that claims to be an aggregate — `total*`, `*Supply`, `*Balance`, `*Deposited`, `*Locked`, `*Reserve`, `*Debt`, `*Accrued`, indices, cumulative rates — enumerate **every** function that writes it and whether that write increases or decreases it.
1691	
1692	Then build the asymmetry table. Three columns of pure gold:
1693	
1694	| Asymmetry | What to look for | Real finding |
1695	| --- | --- | --- |
1696	| Moved without tracking | value transferred out with no matching decrement | *"Users redeeming early will withdraw `Ra` without decreasing the amount locked, which will lead to stolen funds when withdrawing after expiry"* |
1697	| Tracked in one branch only | `if` updates the total, `else` does not | *"Users will steal excess funds from the Vault due to `VaultPoolLib::redeem()` not always decreasing `raBalance` and `paBalance`"* |
1698	| Never tracked at all | a balance is real but no variable represents it | *"Total `ETH`, `WETH` and `gameETH` are not tracked which will lead to insolvency"* |
1699	
1700	Also flag every place a **live balance read** (`token.balanceOf(address(this))`, `address(this).balance`) is used as an accounting source. That is a donation attack or a cross-user theft waiting to happen — *"`ManagedLeveragedVault::openDen()` using all `asset()` balance"*, *"SDAIPriceFeed is vulnerable to donation attack via manipulatable vault rate"*.
1701	
1702	## Phase 2 — Write the invariants down
1703	
1704	5–15 statements that must always hold. Concretely, not vaguely:
1705	
1706	- `Σ(all user withdrawable) <= actual token balance` — the solvency invariant, his single most productive one
1707	- `totalX == Σ userX` for every aggregate with a per-user counterpart
1708	- every credited unit is debited exactly once, in exactly one place
1709	- monotonic things (indices, cumulative rates, timestamps) never go backwards and cannot be advanced for free
1710	- a user's claim cannot increase from an action that costs them nothing
1711	- state on chain A and chain B agree after every message settles
1712	
1713	An invariant you can state and then break with a sequence is a finding. An invariant the docs assert and the code does not enforce is his highest-yield source of all.
1714	
1715	## Phase 3 — Run the lifecycles, not the functions
1716	
1717	Do not audit function by function. Audit *sequences*, and after each step write down which accounting variables changed and which should have.
1718	
1719	Canonical sequences to run:
1720	
1721	1. deposit → accrue yield → withdraw
1722	2. deposit → borrow → price moves → liquidate → withdraw
1723	3. stake → rewards distributed → unstake → claim
1724	4. deposit → withdraw → deposit again (re-entry into the same accounting slot — *"Borrower deposit, withdraw, deposit will reinit `omniChainData.cdsPoolValue`"*)
1725	5. open → adjust position → close (does the adjust path keep every invariant the open path established? — *"The health of a `ProtectedListing` is incorrectly calculated if `tokenTaken` has been changed through `adjustPosition()`"*)
1726	6. source chain send → destination chain receive → failure/retry
1727	7. the same sequence at expiry / after maturity / after the vault has ended
1728	
1729	For each, ask at every step: **what did we just change that something else still assumes the old value of?**
1730	
1731	## Phase 4 — Attack across cohorts and across time
1732	
1733	This is the most distinctive part of his method, and the least commonly imitated.
1734	
1735	Value in DeFi is split pro-rata among a changing set of holders. Any calculation that uses a *current* total to distribute a *historically accumulated* amount lets someone join late and take a share of value they did not earn.
1736	
1737	Three questions, applied to every distribution, reward, fee, yield, and profit path:
1738	
1739	1. **Can I join immediately before a distribution and take a share of it?**
1740	   *"Immediately start getting rewards belonging to others after staking"*, *"Late abond holders steal USDa amount from liquidations from earlier abond holders"*, *"increaseNetworkTotal() allows big arbitrage opportunities by depositing before an increase transaction"*
1741	2. **Can I leave immediately before a loss and push it onto whoever stays?**
1742	   *"Borrower withdrawing at a loss will cause losses for cds depositors that only withdraw after the price recovers"*
1743	3. **The Last User Out test.** Have every user withdraw, in sequence, in the worst order. Does the last one get paid? If the protocol is short by even dust, the money map has a leak upstream — go find it.
1744	   *"`totalEarnings` is incorrect when withdrawing after ending which will withdraw too many funds leaving the `Vault` insolvent"*
1745	
1746	Cumulative-rate and index-based accounting deserves special hostility: check whether the index can be advanced without cost (*"Malicious user can call `calculateCumulativeRate()` any number of times to inflate debt rate as `lastEventTime` is not updated"*), and whether a user's snapshot is taken at the right moment (*"Depositing to another receiver other than `msg.sender` will lead to stuck funds by increasing `avgStart` without claiming"*).
1747	
1748	## Phase 5 — Saturate the subsystem
1749	
1750	When you find one bug, **do not move on**. His reports cluster: 38 findings in one protocol, most in a single accounting subsystem. That is not luck. Once the accounting model is in your head, mine it out.
1751	
1752	After every finding:
1753	1. Search the codebase for every other site with the same code shape — by function name *and* by pattern. If `redeem()` forgets a decrement, check `withdraw()`, `emergencyWithdraw()`, `redeemExpired()`, and the cross-chain variant.
1754	2. Attack the other branches of the function where you found it.
1755	3. Escalate: a DoS often conceals fund theft; a rounding error often compounds into drain. Push each finding to its worst exploitable variant before writing it up.
1756	
1757	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure, not an omission.
1758	
1759	## Phase 6 — Prove it, with preconditions stated honestly
1760	
1761	His writeups make the reader's job trivial by separating what the protocol must look like from what the world must look like:
1762	
1763	- **Internal pre-conditions** — protocol state required (a maturity exists, a position is near liquidation, deposits are non-zero). "None" is common and is the strongest possible case.
1764	- **External pre-conditions** — market/oracle/chain conditions required (price moves X%, sequencer down, gas above Y). "None" is again the strongest case.
1765	- **Attack path** — numbered, concrete, with actors and numbers. Not "an attacker could manipulate the rate" but "1. User deposits 100e18. 2. User is liquidated via `liquidationType1()`, adding 5e18 USDa. 3. Attacker deposits via flashloan and withdraws, taking 4.9e18 of it."
1766	- **Impact** — who loses what. Name the victim class.
1767	
1768	If you cannot fill the attack path with real numbers, you have a LEAD. Say so. A well-described lead is worth more than a finding you inflated.
1769	
1770	## Phase 7 — Minimal mitigation
1771	
1772	One change, the smallest that removes the defect, stated in the protocol's own terms:
1773	
1774	- "Add a cumulative tracking variable to handle this case."
1775	- "Set the vesting interest to 0 when the new interest is 0."
1776	- "Decrease `raBalance` in the early-redemption branch as well."
1777	- "Use `mulDiv` when converting between token and share amounts."
1778	
1779	Not "refactor the accounting system." Not "consider adding validation." Name the operation to add, remove, or reorder.
1780	
1781	## Three habits that separate his findings from noise
1782	
1783	**Root cause is a missing operation at a named line.** Very often the bug is not a wrong line but an absent one. Write it that way: *"In `PsmLib.sol:125`, `self.psm.balances.ra.decLocked(amount)` is not called."* Pointing at the absence is what makes the fix obvious.
1784	
1785	**Judge what the code allows, never what the deployer intends.** "The admin wouldn't do that" is not a mitigation. But equally, "admin can rug" with no concrete mechanism is not a finding.
1786	
1787	**Doubt the clean-looking path hardest.** The functions that read as obviously correct are the ones everyone else also skipped. When a guard looks sufficient, name three specific ways to defeat it — with addresses, values, and states, not abstractions — before you accept it.
1788	
1789	## Do not report
1790	
1791	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Standard, accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a swap the user chose, rounding dust with no amplification, first-depositor inflation where `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` or a virtual-share offset is already present). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" with no mechanism. Gas optimizations dressed as vulnerabilities. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters.
1792	# Lens 5 — Cross-Chain & Asynchronous State
1793	
1794	You own every message that crosses a trust or latency boundary: LayerZero, CCIP, Connext, native bridges, and any request/callback pair where state is written on one side and read on the other.
1795	
1796	If the protocol is single-chain and fully synchronous, say so explicitly and spend your effort on the request/callback and escrow paths instead — the same failure modes appear wherever an action is split across two transactions.
1797	
1798	## The shape
1799	
1800	Two chains hold copies of a "global" state. Messages are asynchronous, can arrive out of order, can fail, and can be sent by anyone with the right payload. Any design that treats the remote write as immediate, ordered, or atomic with the local write is broken — and the resulting desync is permanent because there is no path that reconciles it.
1801	
1802	## Attack surfaces
1803	
1804	**Non-atomic global state.** The core LayerZero/CCIP failure: chain A updates a global aggregate and sends it to chain B, while chain B does the same. Whichever message lands last overwrites the other's update, silently destroying it.
1805	> *Using LayerZero for synchronizing global states between two chains may lead to overwriting of global states*
1806	> *`borrowing::liquidate()` sends the wrong liquidation index to the destination chain, overwriting liquidation information and getting collateral stuck*
1807	> *Cds amounts to reduce from each chain are incorrect and will lead to the inability to withdraw cds in one of the chains*
1808	
1809	**Value debited here, credited nowhere.** If the destination handler can revert — for any reason, including gas, a paused token, a blacklist, or an unset peer — the source funds are already gone. Enumerate every revert in the receive path and ask what happens to the debited amount.
1810	> *Exercise option cross chain message in the (m)TapiocaOFT will always revert in the destination, losing debited funds in the source chain*
1811	> *Users will lock raffle prizes on the `WinnablesPrizeManager` contract by calling `WinnablesTicketManager::propagateRaffleWinner` with wrong CCIP inputs*
1812	> *Attacker can block LayerZero channel due to missing check of minimum gas passed*
1813	> *Send should revert if the gas limit has not been set for a destination chain (peer)*
1814	
1815	**Unvalidated message parameters.** The payload is attacker-controlled unless proven otherwise. Check the sender, the source chain, the peer registration, the recipient, and every amount/share field independently — a mismatch between an amount field and a shares field is a classic drain.
1816	> *All assets of (m)TapiocaOFT can be stolen by depositing to strategy cross chain call with 1 amount but maximum shares possible*
1817	> *TOFT in (m)TapiocaOft contracts can be stolen by calling `removeCollateral()` with a malicious `removeParams.market`*
1818	> *`triggerSendFrom()` will send all the ETH in the destination chain to the `refundAddress` in the LzCallParams argument*
1819	> *NFTs can be stolen by calling `send()` and receiving the nfts in another chain*
1820	
1821	**Address assumptions across chains.** The same address is not the same entity on every chain. Smart wallets, contracts deployed with different nonces, and CREATE2 with different init code all break the "send to msg.sender on the other side" pattern.
1822	> *Lost nfts due to smart wallets having different addresses on different chains*
1823	> *AaveETHYieldBackend uses wrong WETH address for Polygon (returns WETH instead of WPOL)*
1824	
1825	**Fees and gas asymmetry.** Fees quoted on the source chain rarely equal costs on the destination. Charging symmetric fees, hardcoding gas limits, or forgetting to forward `msg.value` for the message fee all fail.
1826	> *`GlobalVariables::oftOrCollateralReceiveFromOtherChains()` calculates the fee as if it was the same in both chains, which is false*
1827	> *`GlobalVariables::oftOrCollateralReceiveFromOtherChains()` always charges twice the collateral on `COLLATERAL_TRANSFER`, which is not needed*
1828	> *mTapiocaOFT can't be rebalanced because the Balancer calls `swapETH()` or `swap()` of the RouterETH but does not forward ether for the message fee*
1829	> *BlsBn254 is not available in certain chains due to hardcoded gas limit*
1830	
1831	**Yield and collateral on the wrong chain.** When a protocol tracks positions on one chain and assets on another, verify every update lands where the asset actually is.
1832	> *`treasury.updateYieldsFromLiquidatedLrts()` updates the yield in the current chain, but collateral may be in the other chain*
1833	
1834	**Callbacks and retries.** Failed-message retry paths, `executeFailedWithUpdatedArgs`, and generic callback handlers are entry points with the weakest validation in the codebase. Treat them as fully permissionless until proven otherwise, and check for reentrancy into the main accounting.
1835	> *ConnextHandler `executeFailedWithUpdatedArgs(...)` reentrancy allowedCaller can steal all ConnextHandler tokens*
1836	> *Funds may be stolen by calling `onMoreFlashLoan()` directly*
1837	> *In BaseRouter, the beneficiary isn't checked when starting a flashloan action and it replaces the previous beneficiary*
1838	
1839	**Self-destruct and upgrade exposure on proxied modules.** Module contracts reached by delegatecall inherit the caller's storage and can be destroyed or reinitialized.
1840	> *TOFT and USDO Modules Can Be Selfdestructed*
1841	
1842	## Every finding needs the two-chain trace
1843	
1844	State the ordering explicitly: what chain A does, what chain B does, in which order the messages land, and what the two states are afterwards. Name the value that is now unrecoverable.
1845	# Shared Lens Rules
1846	
1847	## Bundle contents
1848	
1849	Your bundle is five concatenated parts: all in-scope source, the protocol's **money map** (built by the orchestrator), the **method** (how to think), your **lens** (what you own), and these shared rules (output format and protocol).
1850	
1851	Read the whole bundle once at the start. Do not re-read in-scope files for the initial scan. Read or search the repo only for cross-file lookups or out-of-scope context (`interfaces/`, `lib/`, `mocks/`, `test/`).
1852	
1853	**Start from the money map, not the file list.** Pick the tracked totals, lifecycles, and cohorts your lens owns, and attack those. The file list is where you go to confirm, not where you begin.
1854	
1855	When matching function names, check both `functionName` and `_functionName` (Solidity convention), and check library variants (`XLib::function`).
1856	
1857	## Public audit-evidence summaries
1858	
1859	Provide concise public audit evidence and final conclusions, with source references. Do not provide private working text, hidden chain-of-thought, or a transcript of internal deliberation. The following labels organize the public report; they are not instructions to reveal private reasoning or to emit intermediate working text before continuing.
1860	
1861	| Evidence category | Public label | Brief report content |
1862	| --- | --- | --- |
1863	| A function moves value or writes a tracked total | `[Model: <name>]` | Summarize what a user gives, what they receive, and the totals changed, citing the relevant function. |
1864	| A non-obvious operation relies on an assumption | `[Why: <file:line>]` | State the relevant assumption and the source evidence establishing it, or identify the unresolved assumption. |
1865	| An access guard or value-moving path is assessed | `[Defeat: <function>]` | Report concise boundary-test or adversarial-case outcomes and the effective guard or uncovered condition; no private deliberation is requested. |
1866	| A lifecycle is assessed | `[LastOut: <lifecycle>]` | State the conservation/liability result and whether all eligible users can receive the amounts owed, with evidence or a clearly identified gap. |
1867	
1868	Use these summaries as public evidence for the audit result. The orchestrator may inventory which evidence categories were covered; it must not request or evaluate private reasoning traces. 1869	
1870	## Saturation is mandatory
1871	
1872	When you find a bug, weaponize the pattern across the entire codebase before moving on. Search by function name AND by code shape. If one redemption path forgets a decrement, check every other redemption, withdrawal, emergency, expiry, and cross-chain variant. Then attack the other branches of the function where you found it. Then escalate the finding to its worst exploitable variant — a DoS often hides fund theft.
1873	
1874	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure.
1875	
1876	## Do not report
1877	
1878	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a user-chosen swap, rounding dust with no amplification path, first-depositor inflation where a virtual-share offset or `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` already exists). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" or "admin can rug" without a concrete mechanism. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters. Gas findings.
1879	
1880	## Output
1881	
1882	FINDINGs have a concrete, unguarded, exploitable path with a named victim. LEADs have a real accounting or logic smell with a partial path. Default to LEAD over dropping — never drop.
1883	
1884	**One vulnerability per block.** Same root cause = one block. Needs a different fix = separate block.
1885	
1886	```
1887	FINDING | contract: Name | function: func | bug_class: kebab-tag | group_key: Contract | function | bug-class
1888	root_cause: the defect at File.sol:LINE, naming the missing or wrong operation
1889	internal_pre: protocol state required, or None
1890	external_pre: market/oracle/chain conditions required, or None
1891	path:
1892	  1. actor does X with concrete amount
1893	  2. state changes to Y
1894	  3. actor does Z
1895	impact: who loses what, and who is left holding the loss
1896	mitigation: the single smallest change that removes the defect
1897	```
1898	
1899	```
1900	LEAD | contract: Name | function: func | bug_class: kebab-tag | group_key: Contract | function | bug-class
1901	smell: what you found
1902	unverified: precisely what you could not establish
1903	description: one sentence on the trail
1904	```
1905	
1906	`group_key` drives deduplication and is always `ContractName | functionName | bug_class`.
1907	
1908	An `internal_pre` or `external_pre` of `None` is the strongest possible finding — never pad these to look thorough. State the truth.

814	// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT

816	
817	import { IVRFV2PlusWrapper } from "@chainlink/contracts/src/v0.8/vrf/dev/interfaces/IVRFV2PlusWrapper.sol";
818	import { IERC20 } from "@openzeppelin/contracts/token/ERC20/IERC20.sol";
819	import { IERC721 } from "@openzeppelin/contracts/token/ERC721/IERC721.sol";
820	
821	/// @title raffle.fun Raffle Interface
822	/// @author heesho
823	/// @notice Defines one autonomous NFT raffle using fixed-price USDC entries and one transferable ERC-721 ticket per
824	///         purchase.
825	/// @dev Ticket IDs are sequential. Each ticket stores one inclusive uint128 entry range and remains a transferable
826	///      bearer claim until its owner atomically burns it for redemption or refund. The immutable quote token is trusted
827	///      canonical six-decimal USDC with standard, non-rebasing, fee-free transfers. Supported prizes are honest,
828	///      standards-compliant ERC-721s.
829	/// @custom:version 1.0.0
830	interface IRaffle {
831	    // Types
832	
833	    /// @notice The single authoritative raffle lifecycle and economic result.
834	    enum Status {
835	        /// @notice The clone is initialized and waiting for the factory to escrow the configured prize.
836	        AwaitingPrize,
837	        /// @notice The prize is escrowed and entry sales or post-sale draw initiation are available.
838	        Active,
839	        /// @notice A Chainlink VRF request was accepted and its callback window is open.
840	        Drawing,
841	        /// @notice The reserve was met and the winning ticket may redeem the prize NFT.
842	        NftWon,
843	        /// @notice The reserve was missed and the winning ticket may redeem its cash allocation.
844	        CashWon,
845	        /// @notice Full ticket refunds are enabled and the sponsor may recover the prize NFT.
846	        Refunding
847	    }
848	
849	    /// @notice Complete clone-specific configuration supplied once by the canonical factory.
850	    /// @param sponsor Prize depositor and empty-raffle cancellation authority.
851	    /// @param sponsorRecipient Immutable recipient of sponsor quote proceeds and any returned prize.
852	    /// @param protocolTreasury Immutable recipient of protocol fees.
853	    /// @param prizeToken Standards-compliant ERC-721 prize contract.
854	    /// @param prizeTokenId Token ID of the prize escrowed by this raffle.
855	    /// @param raffleId One-based canonical factory identifier for this raffle.
856	    /// @param reserveEntries Global raw entry-count threshold selecting the NFT outcome when met or exceeded.
857	    /// @param endTime Unix timestamp, in seconds, at which entry sales end exclusively.
858	    struct RaffleInitParams {
859	        address sponsor;
860	        address sponsorRecipient;
861	        address protocolTreasury;
862	        address prizeToken;
863	        uint256 prizeTokenId;
864	        uint256 raffleId;
865	        uint128 reserveEntries;
866	        uint64 endTime;
867	    }
868	
869	    // Events
870	
871	    /// @notice Emitted when the factory deposits the configured prize and activates the raffle.
872	    /// @param prizeToken ERC-721 contract of the deposited prize.
873	    /// @param prizeTokenId Token ID of the deposited prize.
874	    /// @param sponsor Address that deposited the prize through the factory.
875	    event PrizeDeposited(address indexed prizeToken, uint256 indexed prizeTokenId, address indexed sponsor);
876	
877	    /// @notice Emitted when a buyer pays for entries and one range ticket is minted.
878	    /// @param buyer Address that paid the six-decimal quote-token amount.
879	    /// @param recipient Address that received the newly minted ticket.
880	    /// @param ticketId Sequential ticket ID assigned to the purchase.
881	    /// @param firstEntry First global raffle entry represented by the ticket, inclusive.
882	    /// @param lastEntry Last global raffle entry represented by the ticket, inclusive.
883	    /// @param entryCount Number of entries represented by the ticket.
884	    /// @param grossAmount Raw six-decimal quote-token units paid, equal to `entryCount * ENTRY_PRICE`.
885	    event TicketPurchased(
886	        address indexed buyer,
887	        address indexed recipient,
888	        uint256 indexed ticketId,
889	        uint128 firstEntry,
890	        uint128 lastEntry,
891	        uint128 entryCount,
892	        uint256 grossAmount
893	    );
894	
895	    /// @notice Emitted when the raffle pays for and records its one Chainlink VRF request.
896	    /// @param requestId Wrapper-assigned request identifier.
897	    /// @param requester Address that initiated and funded the request.
898	    /// @param fee Native-token wei actually paid to the wrapper for the request.
899	    /// @param excessReturned Native-token wei returned to the requester after paying the actual fee.
900	    /// @param drawRequestedAt Unix timestamp, in seconds, when the request was accepted.
901	    /// @param callbackDeadline Exclusive Unix-timestamp deadline for accepting the authenticated callback.
902	    event DrawRequested(
903	        uint256 indexed requestId,
904	        address indexed requester,
905	        uint256 fee,
906	        uint256 excessReturned,
907	        uint256 drawRequestedAt,
908	        uint256 callbackDeadline
909	    );
910	
911	    /// @notice Emitted when an authenticated, ABI-decodable callback cannot resolve the raffle.
912	    /// @param receivedRequestId Request ID supplied by the wrapper callback.
913	    /// @param expectedRequestId Request ID currently recorded by the raffle, or zero before request persistence.
914	    /// @param status Current raffle status when the callback is ignored.
915	    event VrfCallbackIgnored(uint256 indexed receivedRequestId, uint256 indexed expectedRequestId, Status status);
916	
917	    /// @notice Emitted when an authenticated callback selects the winning entry and final result.
918	    /// @param requestId Request ID that produced the accepted randomness.
919	    /// @param winningEntry Selected one-based global entry number in `[1,totalEntries]`.
920	    /// @param result Final `NftWon` or `CashWon` result.
921	    event RaffleResolved(uint256 indexed requestId, uint128 indexed winningEntry, Status indexed result);
922	
923	    /// @notice Emitted when the raffle enters the full-refund branch.
924	    /// @param finalizer Address that enabled refunds.
925	    /// @param remainingRefundLiability Raw six-decimal quote-token units initially available for ticket refunds.
926	    event RefundsEnabled(address indexed finalizer, uint256 remainingRefundLiability);
927	
928	    /// @notice Emitted when the winning ticket is proven and all terminal quote-token liabilities are allocated.
929	    /// @param ticketId Ticket proven to contain the selected winning entry.
930	    /// @param settler Address that performed permissionless settlement.
931	    /// @param result Final `NftWon` or `CashWon` result.
932	    /// @param cashAmount Raw six-decimal quote-token units allocated to the cash winner; zero for `NftWon`.
933	    /// @param protocolFee Raw six-decimal quote-token units allocated to the treasury, rounded down from gross sales.
934	    /// @param sponsorAmount Raw six-decimal quote-token units allocated to the sponsor recipient as the remainder.
935	    event WinningTicketSettled(
936	        uint256 indexed ticketId,
937	        address indexed settler,
938	        Status indexed result,
939	        uint256 cashAmount,
940	        uint256 protocolFee,
941	        uint256 sponsorAmount
942	    );
943	
944	    /// @notice Emitted when the winning ticket owner burns the ticket and receives the corresponding prize.
945	    /// @param ticketId Burned winning ticket ID.
946	    /// @param winner Ticket owner that received the prize at redemption time.
947	    /// @param result Final `NftWon` or `CashWon` result.
948	    /// @param cashAmount Raw six-decimal quote-token units paid for `CashWon`; zero for `NftWon`.
949	    /// @param prizeToken ERC-721 prize contract for `NftWon`; the zero address for `CashWon`.
950	    /// @param prizeTokenId ERC-721 prize token ID for `NftWon`; zero for `CashWon`.
951	    event WinningTicketRedeemed(
952	        uint256 indexed ticketId,
953	        address indexed winner,
954	        Status indexed result,
955	        uint256 cashAmount,
956	        address prizeToken,
957	        uint256 prizeTokenId
958	    );
959	
960	    /// @notice Emitted when an owner burns one or more tickets for a full quote-token refund.
961	    /// @param owner Ticket owner that burned the tickets and received the refund.
962	    /// @param ticketQuantity Number of tickets burned in this transaction.
963	    /// @param entryQuantity Aggregate number of entries represented by the burned tickets.
964	    /// @param amount Raw six-decimal quote-token units refunded, equal to `entryQuantity * ENTRY_PRICE`.
965	    /// @param remainingRefundLiability Raw six-decimal quote-token units still claimable after this refund.
966	    event TicketsRefunded(
967	        address indexed owner,
968	        uint256 ticketQuantity,
969	        uint256 entryQuantity,
970	        uint256 amount,
971	        uint256 remainingRefundLiability
972	    );
973	
974	    /// @notice Emitted when the complete current sponsor balance is released to its immutable recipient.
975	    /// @param caller Address that triggered the permissionless release.
976	    /// @param recipient Immutable sponsor recipient that received the payment.
977	    /// @param amount Raw six-decimal quote-token units paid.
978	    event SponsorProceedsReleased(address indexed caller, address indexed recipient, uint256 amount);
979	
980	    /// @notice Emitted when the complete current protocol-fee balance is released to the immutable treasury.
981	    /// @param caller Address that triggered the permissionless release.
982	    /// @param treasury Immutable protocol treasury that received the payment.
983	    /// @param amount Raw six-decimal quote-token units paid.
984	    event ProtocolFeesReleased(address indexed caller, address indexed treasury, uint256 amount);
985

1544	Ethereum NFT raffle; immutable factory, ERC-1167 clones with immutable implementation. One entry costs 1,000,000 units of canonical six-decimal USDC. 1647	# The 0xSimao Method
1648	
1649	Derived from 869 published findings across 143 reviews. This is HOW to think. Your lens file is WHAT to look for. Work them together.
1650	
1651	## The core thesis
1652	
1653	Most auditors read code looking for bad lines. That finds the bugs a linter finds.
1654	
1655	0xSimao reads code looking for **a claim that has drifted from what actually backs it**. Value moves through a protocol in sequences: deposit, accrue, borrow, liquidate, withdraw. Each step writes some subset of the accounting state, and drift is any way that state stops describing reality:
1656	
1657	| Drift | Shape |
1658	| --- | --- |
1659	| The write is missing | value moved and no variable recorded it — or one branch updates it and the sibling branch does not |
1660	| The write is wrong | the variable is updated with the wrong amount, direction, rounding, units, or decimals |
1661	| The write is mistimed | the right value at the wrong moment, so someone's snapshot is taken against state that is about to change |
1662	| The write goes to the wrong party | the total is intact; the split between cohorts is not |
1663	| The input was never trustworthy | the number is faithfully propagated from an oracle, a live balance, or a caller-supplied parameter an attacker controls |
1664	| The state is unreachable | the accounting is correct but a revert, a pause, an unbounded loop, or a missing path means it can never be settled |
1665	
1666	The drift is invisible at any single line. It only appears when you ask: *after this whole sequence, does the protocol still owe exactly what it holds — and can everyone actually collect it?*
1667	
1668	A defect nobody can be shown to lose money from is a curiosity. So every candidate gets one more question, and it is the one that separates a finding from a smell:
1669	
1670	> **Who is left holding the loss?**
1671	
1672	Answer with a named class of actor, never "users". For accounting drift it is often whoever withdraws last, because a shortfall stays invisible until the balance runs out — but for a bricked liquidation it is the solvent lenders eating the bad debt, for a mistimed snapshot it is the cohort that held through the accrual, and for a forged signature it is whoever the forged message was drawn against. If the only person worse off is the caller, there is no finding.
1673	
1674	**This lens is the sharpest one, not the only one.** Accounting drift is the largest single class in his corpus, but it is not the majority of it. The rest is DoS and permanently stuck funds, access control and signature defects, token- and integration-behaviour assumptions (`USDT` approvals, fee-on-transfer, blacklists, pausable collateral), oracle and parameter validation, and cross-chain state — and those are what your lens file owns. Work the money map first because it is what makes the drift class visible; then work your lens on its own terms. When the target has little accounting to speak of — a router, a registry, a verifier, a signature scheme — say so, keep the money map short, and go straight to your lens. Do not force a finding into the drift frame to make it sound like his.
1675	
1676	## Phase 0 — Learn the protocol's own vocabulary before reading for bugs
1677	
1678	His findings are written in the protocol's language: `cdsPoolValue`, `abond`, `downsideProtected`, `unassignedEarnings`, `raBalance`, `floatingBackupBorrowed`. He does not audit "a vault"; he audits *this* vault's specific accounting model.
1679	
1680	Before hunting, be able to state in plain English:
1681	- What does a user give, and what claim do they receive in return?
1682	- What is that claim worth, and which variables determine the value?
1683	- Where does yield come from, and who is entitled to it?
1684	- What happens when the protocol is short — who absorbs the shortfall?
1685	
1686	If you cannot answer these without Solidity jargon, you are not ready to find his class of bug. Any spot where your plain-English explanation goes fuzzy is exactly where the bug is; mark it and come back.
1687	
1688	## Phase 1 — Build the money map
1689	
1690	For every storage variable that claims to be an aggregate — `total*`, `*Supply`, `*Balance`, `*Deposited`, `*Locked`, `*Reserve`, `*Debt`, `*Accrued`, indices, cumulative rates — enumerate **every** function that writes it and whether that write increases or decreases it.
1691	
1692	Then build the asymmetry table. Three columns of pure gold:
1693	
1694	| Asymmetry | What to look for | Real finding |
1695	| --- | --- | --- |
1696	| Moved without tracking | value transferred out with no matching decrement | *"Users redeeming early will withdraw `Ra` without decreasing the amount locked, which will lead to stolen funds when withdrawing after expiry"* |
1697	| Tracked in one branch only | `if` updates the total, `else` does not | *"Users will steal excess funds from the Vault due to `VaultPoolLib::redeem()` not always decreasing `raBalance` and `paBalance`"* |
1698	| Never tracked at all | a balance is real but no variable represents it | *"Total `ETH`, `WETH` and `gameETH` are not tracked which will lead to insolvency"* |
1699	
1700	Also flag every place a **live balance read** (`token.balanceOf(address(this))`, `address(this).balance`) is used as an accounting source. That is a donation attack or a cross-user theft waiting to happen — *"`ManagedLeveragedVault::openDen()` using all `asset()` balance"*, *"SDAIPriceFeed is vulnerable to donation attack via manipulatable vault rate"*.
1701	
1702	## Phase 2 — Write the invariants down
1703	
1704	5–15 statements that must always hold. Concretely, not vaguely:
1705	
1706	- `Σ(all user withdrawable) <= actual token balance` — the solvency invariant, his single most productive one
1707	- `totalX == Σ userX` for every aggregate with a per-user counterpart
1708	- every credited unit is debited exactly once, in exactly one place
1709	- monotonic things (indices, cumulative rates, timestamps) never go backwards and cannot be advanced for free
1710	- a user's claim cannot increase from an action that costs them nothing
1711	- state on chain A and chain B agree after every message settles
1712	
1713	An invariant you can state and then break with a sequence is a finding. An invariant the docs assert and the code does not enforce is his highest-yield source of all.
1714	
1715	## Phase 3 — Run the lifecycles, not the functions
1716	
1717	Do not audit function by function. Audit *sequences*, and after each step write down which accounting variables changed and which should have.
1718	
1719	Canonical sequences to run:
1720	
1721	1. deposit → accrue yield → withdraw
1722	2. deposit → borrow → price moves → liquidate → withdraw
1723	3. stake → rewards distributed → unstake → claim
1724	4. deposit → withdraw → deposit again (re-entry into the same accounting slot — *"Borrower deposit, withdraw, deposit will reinit `omniChainData.cdsPoolValue`"*)
1725	5. open → adjust position → close (does the adjust path keep every invariant the open path established? — *"The health of a `ProtectedListing` is incorrectly calculated if `tokenTaken` has been changed through `adjustPosition()`"*)
1726	6. source chain send → destination chain receive → failure/retry
1727	7. the same sequence at expiry / after maturity / after the vault has ended
1728	
1729	For each, ask at every step: **what did we just change that something else still assumes the old value of?**
1730	
1731	## Phase 4 — Attack across cohorts and across time
1732	
1733	This is the most distinctive part of his method, and the least commonly imitated.
1734	
1735	Value in DeFi is split pro-rata among a changing set of holders. Any calculation that uses a *current* total to distribute a *historically accumulated* amount lets someone join late and take a share of value they did not earn.
1736	
1737	Three questions, applied to every distribution, reward, fee, yield, and profit path:
1738	
1739	1. **Can I join immediately before a distribution and take a share of it?**
1740	   *"Immediately start getting rewards belonging to others after staking"*, *"Late abond holders steal USDa amount from liquidations from earlier abond holders"*, *"increaseNetworkTotal() allows big arbitrage opportunities by depositing before an increase transaction"*
1741	2. **Can I leave immediately before a loss and push it onto whoever stays?**
1742	   *"Borrower withdrawing at a loss will cause losses for cds depositors that only withdraw after the price recovers"*
1743	3. **The Last User Out test.** Have every user withdraw, in sequence, in the worst order. Does the last one get paid? If the protocol is short by even dust, the money map has a leak upstream — go find it.
1744	   *"`totalEarnings` is incorrect when withdrawing after ending which will withdraw too many funds leaving the `Vault` insolvent"*
1745	
1746	Cumulative-rate and index-based accounting deserves special hostility: check whether the index can be advanced without cost (*"Malicious user can call `calculateCumulativeRate()` any number of times to inflate debt rate as `lastEventTime` is not updated"*), and whether a user's snapshot is taken at the right moment (*"Depositing to another receiver other than `msg.sender` will lead to stuck funds by increasing `avgStart` without claiming"*).
1747	
1748	## Phase 5 — Saturate the subsystem
1749	
1750	When you find one bug, **do not move on**. His reports cluster: 38 findings in one protocol, most in a single accounting subsystem. That is not luck. Once the accounting model is in your head, mine it out.
1751	
1752	After every finding:
1753	1. Search the codebase for every other site with the same code shape — by function name *and* by pattern. If `redeem()` forgets a decrement, check `withdraw()`, `emergencyWithdraw()`, `redeemExpired()`, and the cross-chain variant.
1754	2. Attack the other branches of the function where you found it.
1755	3. Escalate: a DoS often conceals fund theft; a rounding error often compounds into drain. Push each finding to its worst exploitable variant before writing it up.
1756	
1757	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure, not an omission.
1758	
1759	## Phase 6 — Prove it, with preconditions stated honestly
1760	
1761	His writeups make the reader's job trivial by separating what the protocol must look like from what the world must look like:
1762	
1763	- **Internal pre-conditions** — protocol state required (a maturity exists, a position is near liquidation, deposits are non-zero). "None" is common and is the strongest possible case.
1764	- **External pre-conditions** — market/oracle/chain conditions required (price moves X%, sequencer down, gas above Y). "None" is again the strongest case.
1765	- **Attack path** — numbered, concrete, with actors and numbers. Not "an attacker could manipulate the rate" but "1. User deposits 100e18. 2. User is liquidated via `liquidationType1()`, adding 5e18 USDa. 3. Attacker deposits via flashloan and withdraws, taking 4.9e18 of it."
1766	- **Impact** — who loses what. Name the victim class.
1767	
1768	If you cannot fill the attack path with real numbers, you have a LEAD. Say so. A well-described lead is worth more than a finding you inflated.
1769	
1770	## Phase 7 — Minimal mitigation
1771	
1772	One change, the smallest that removes the defect, stated in the protocol's own terms:
1773	
1774	- "Add a cumulative tracking variable to handle this case."
1775	- "Set the vesting interest to 0 when the new interest is 0."
1776	- "Decrease `raBalance` in the early-redemption branch as well."
1777	- "Use `mulDiv` when converting between token and share amounts."
1778	
1779	Not "refactor the accounting system." Not "consider adding validation." Name the operation to add, remove, or reorder.
1780	
1781	## Three habits that separate his findings from noise
1782	
1783	**Root cause is a missing operation at a named line.** Very often the bug is not a wrong line but an absent one. Write it that way: *"In `PsmLib.sol:125`, `self.psm.balances.ra.decLocked(amount)` is not called."* Pointing at the absence is what makes the fix obvious.
1784	
1785	**Judge what the code allows, never what the deployer intends.** "The admin wouldn't do that" is not a mitigation. But equally, "admin can rug" with no concrete mechanism is not a finding.
1786	
1787	**Doubt the clean-looking path hardest.** The functions that read as obviously correct are the ones everyone else also skipped. When a guard looks sufficient, name three specific ways to defeat it — with addresses, values, and states, not abstractions — before you accept it.
1788	
1789	## Do not report
1790	
1791	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Standard, accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a swap the user chose, rounding dust with no amplification, first-depositor inflation where `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` or a virtual-share offset is already present). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" with no mechanism. Gas optimizations dressed as vulnerabilities. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters.
1792	# Lens 6 — Rounding, Precision & Scale
1793	
1794	You own integer arithmetic: rounding direction, truncation, decimals, fixed-point scale, casts, and overflow. Every division is a decision about who absorbs the remainder, and every decision made in the wrong direction is extractable.
1795	
1796	0xSimao's framing is sharper than "there is precision loss": he asks **which party the rounding favors, whether that favoring can be repeated, and whether it compounds.** A rounding error that a user can trigger in a loop is a drain, not a nit.
1797	
1798	## Attack surfaces
1799	
1800	**Establish the correct direction, then check every division.** Deposits round shares DOWN. Withdrawals round assets DOWN. Debt rounds UP. Fees round UP. Anything favoring the user in a repeatable path is extractable; anything favoring the protocol in a *forced* path can be weaponized as griefing or, when the protocol is a counterparty to itself, as a drain.
1801	> *Wrong rounding direction in `StakingPool::unstake()` can be abused*
1802	> *The Rounding Done in Protocol's Favor Can Be Weaponized to Drain the Protocol*
1803	> *Aave rounding behavior allows malicious users to drain accumulated yield via small withdrawals*
1804	> *`TradingLimits::update()` incorrectly only rounds up when `deltaFlowUnits` becomes 0, which will silently increase trading limits*
1805	
1806	**Find division before multiplication.** `a / b * c` truncates early and amplifies the loss. Trace across function boundaries too — a truncated return value multiplied by the caller is the same bug spread over two files. `mulDiv` exists for this; note its absence.
1807	> *`FluidLocker::_getUnlockingPercentage()` divides before multiplying, suffering a significant precision error*
1808	> *`LenderCommitmentGroup_Smart` does not use `mulDiv` when converting between token and share amounts, possibly leading to DoS or loss of funds*
1809	
1810	**Drive results to zero.** Feed 1 wei, 1 share, and 1 second into every calculation. Where do fees truncate to zero? Where does interest accrue nothing? Where does a reward rate become zero and lock the stream permanently? Zero results flip formulas and are frequently permanent.
1811	> *Integer Truncation in Incentive Rate Permanently Locks Unstreamed Rewards*
1812	> *Precision Loss in `notifyRewardAmount` Function Causes Unclaimable RewardToken*
1813	> *Significant rounding errors due to `gameETH` not having precision*
1814	> *Estimated prize draws in TieredLiquidityDistributor are off due to rounding down when calculating the sum, leading to incorrect prizes*
1815	
1816	**Check every decimal assumption.** Hardcoded `1e18` against a 6-decimal token. `18 - decimals` underflowing for >18-decimal tokens. Oracle decimals assumed constant when the feed sets them. A price feed returning 8 decimals fed into 18-decimal math.
1817	> *Decimals of LendingPool don't take into account the offset introduced by VIRTUAL_SHARES*
1818	> *WBTCZapper decimal mismatch causes revert*
1819	> *WBTCZapper precision loss will lead to reverts*
1820	> *`PreDepositVault` does not collect interest for `WBTC`*
1821	
1822	**Overflow the intermediate.** For every `a * b / c`, construct inputs where `a * b` exceeds uint256 before the division rescues it. Uniswap `sqrtPriceX96` math is the classic: squaring it directly overflows for real pools.
1823	> *Performing a direct multiplication in `_getPriceFromSqrtX96` will overflow for some uniswap pools*
1824	
1825	**Break the casts.** `uint256 → uint128/96/64` without a bounds check. Signed/unsigned round trips that drop the sign bit and turn a small negative into an enormous positive. Unsigned subtraction where the operands are not provably ordered.
1826	> *Potential Underflow in `withdrawInterest`*
1827	> *DOS on liquidation type 1 due to underflow in cds profits computation*
1828	> *`state.cumulativeDepositsMultiplierX18` may become 0 or negative, leading to loss of funds*
1829	> *API3 oracle timestamp can be set to future timestamp and block API3 Oracle usage to make code revert in underflow*
1830	
1831	**Check the units of every constant.** A bare number where a time unit belongs is a whole-order-of-magnitude bug and reads as innocuous.
1832	> *`FluidLocker::_getUnlockingPercentage()` uses 540 instead of `540 days` leading to stuck funds as the unlocking percentage will be bigger than `100%` and underflow*
1833	> *`FluidLocker::_getUnlockingPercentage()` incorrectly divides one of the components of the formula by `S`, leading to always having `80%` penalty*
1834	
1835	**Divide by an unconstrained value.** `x / tickSpacing`, `x / totalSupply`, `x / config.value` — construct the input that drives the divisor to zero or one.
1836	
1837	## Every finding needs concrete arithmetic
1838	
1839	Walk the numbers. State the inputs, the intermediate values, the result, and the correct result. Then state the extraction per call and whether it can be looped. Without numbers it is a LEAD, no exceptions.
1840	# Shared Lens Rules
1841	
1842	## Bundle contents
1843	
1844	Your bundle is five concatenated parts: all in-scope source, the protocol's **money map** (built by the orchestrator), the **method** (how to think), your **lens** (what you own), and these shared rules (output format and protocol).
1845	
1846	Read the whole bundle once at the start. Do not re-read in-scope files for the initial scan. Read or search the repo only for cross-file lookups or out-of-scope context (`interfaces/`, `lib/`, `mocks/`, `test/`).
1847	
1848	**Start from the money map, not the file list.** Pick the tracked totals, lifecycles, and cohorts your lens owns, and attack those. The file list is where you go to confirm, not where you begin.
1849	
1850	When matching function names, check both `functionName` and `_functionName` (Solidity convention), and check library variants (`XLib::function`).
1851	
1852	## Public audit-evidence summaries
1853	
1854	Provide concise public audit evidence and final conclusions, with source references. Do not provide private working text, hidden chain-of-thought, or a transcript of internal deliberation. The following labels organize the public report; they are not instructions to reveal private reasoning or to emit intermediate working text before continuing.
1855	
1856	| Evidence category | Public label | Brief report content |
1857	| --- | --- | --- |
1858	| A function moves value or writes a tracked total | `[Model: <name>]` | Summarize what a user gives, what they receive, and the totals changed, citing the relevant function. |
1859	| A non-obvious operation relies on an assumption | `[Why: <file:line>]` | State the relevant assumption and the source evidence establishing it, or identify the unresolved assumption. |
1860	| An access guard or value-moving path is assessed | `[Defeat: <function>]` | Report concise boundary-test or adversarial-case outcomes and the effective guard or uncovered condition; no private deliberation is requested. |
1861	| A lifecycle is assessed | `[LastOut: <lifecycle>]` | State the conservation/liability result and whether all eligible users can receive the amounts owed, with evidence or a clearly identified gap. |
1862	
1863	Use these summaries as public evidence for the audit result. The orchestrator may inventory which evidence categories were covered; it must not request or evaluate private reasoning traces. All remaining lens scope, saturation, finding format, severity, adjudication, proof and reporting rules are unchanged.
1864	
1865	## Saturation is mandatory
1866	
1867	When you find a bug, weaponize the pattern across the entire codebase before moving on. Search by function name AND by code shape. If one redemption path forgets a decrement, check every other redemption, withdrawal, emergency, expiry, and cross-chain variant. Then attack the other branches of the function where you found it. Then escalate the finding to its worst exploitable variant — a DoS often hides fund theft.
1868	
1869	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure.
1870	
1871	## Do not report
1872	
1873	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a user-chosen swap, rounding dust with no amplification path, first-depositor inflation where a virtual-share offset or `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` already exists). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" or "admin can rug" without a concrete mechanism. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters. Gas findings.
1874	
1875	## Output
1876	
1877	FINDINGs have a concrete, unguarded, exploitable path with a named victim. LEADs have a real accounting or logic smell with a partial path. Default to LEAD over dropping — never drop.
1878	
1879	**One vulnerability per block.** Same root cause = one block. Needs a different fix = separate block.
1880	
1881	```
1882	FINDING | contract: Name | function: func | bug_class: kebab-tag | group_key: Contract | function | bug-class
1883	root_cause: the defect at File.sol:LINE, naming the missing or wrong operation
1884	internal_pre: protocol state required, or None
1885	external_pre: market/oracle/chain conditions required, or None
1886	path:
1887	  1. actor does X with concrete amount
1888	  2. state changes to Y
1889	  3. actor does Z
1890	impact: who loses what, and who is left holding the loss
1891	mitigation: the single smallest change that removes the defect
1892	```
1893	
1894	```
1895	LEAD | contract: Name | function: func | bug_class: kebab-tag | group_key: Contract | function | bug-class
1896	smell: what you found
1897	unverified: precisely what you could not establish
1898	description: one sentence on the trail
1899	```
1900	
1901	`group_key` drives deduplication and is always `ContractName | functionName | bug_class`.
1902	
1903	An `internal_pre` or `external_pre` of `None` is the strongest possible finding — never pad these to look thorough. State the truth.

1540	### DESIGN.md (in-scope clean specification)

1542	```markdown
1543	# Clean design specification
1544	Ethereum NFT raffle; immutable factory, ERC-1167 clones with immutable implementation. One entry costs 1,000,000 units of canonical six-decimal USDC. One purchase mints a transferable ERC721 ticket representing a contiguous inclusive range. Exactly one ERC721 prize is escrowed atomically at creation. Reserve met awards NFT and 95% sponsor / 5% treasury. Reserve missed awards 80% gross to winner, 15% sponsor, 5% treasury. Refund outcome pays 100% per entry and returns prize. Rounding is floor on aggregate protocol fee; remainder must be allocated without loss. No administrator, mutable configuration or upgrade. Request window [sale end, end+2days); callback accepted strictly before request timestamp+2days. Refunds open at deadline. Callback records result only. Settlement is permissionless, storage-only; redemption requires current ticket owner, burns claim atomically, and must revert all effects on delivery failure. Sponsor and treasury can claim independently after settlement. Never move assets between raffle clones. Quote token and Chainlink wrapper are trusted canonical dependencies; arbitrary prize contracts and ticket recipients are untrusted. Frontend discovery is advisory; transaction decisions must reread current chain state.
1545	
1546	This specification was composed before scanner results and historical findings. Source, not design prose, determines actual behavior. No tests, audit history, accepted-risk lists or scanner results are provided.
1547	```

CashWon/Refunding: prize leg :404 independent of USDC legs | No state converts an undeliverable NFT into cash/refund. DESIGN.md: "arbitrary prize contracts … are untrusted"; I:14-15 says "Supported prizes are honest, standards-compliant ERC-721s" — conflicting trust statements |
