1600	3. C: in Refunding, `remainingRefundLiability == Σ unburned tickets × 1e6`; the last refunder is paid in full.
1601	4. D: NftWon → NFT to winner, 95% sponsor / 5% treasury. CashWon → 80% gross to winner, 15% sponsor, 5% treasury. Refunding → 100% per entry + prize returned.
1602	5. D: fee floors on the aggregate; remainder allocated without loss (`cash + sponsor + fee == pot`).
1603	6. C: ranges are contiguous, disjoint, cover `[1,totalEntries]`; exactly one ticket contains `winningEntry ∈ [1,totalEntries]`, and that ticket exists unburned at settlement.
1604	7. D/C: the prize leaves exactly once — to the winner iff NftWon, to `sponsorRecipient` iff CashWon or Refunding.
1605	8. C: each ticket is paid at most once (refund XOR winning redemption).
1606	9. C: status is monotone `AwaitingPrize→Active→[Drawing→]{NftWon|CashWon|Refunding}`; terminal states never change; NftWon/CashWon can never reach Refunding.
1607	10. D: request window `[endTime, endTime+2d)`; callback accepted strictly before `drawRequestedAt+2d`; refunds open at the deadline — callback and refund windows are disjoint.
1608	11. D: callback records the result only; settlement is permissionless and storage-only.
1609	12. D: redemption requires the CURRENT ticket owner, burns atomically, and reverts all effects on delivery failure.
1610	13. D: sponsor and treasury claim independently after settlement.
1611	14. D: never move assets between raffle clones; payouts never land on protocol plumbing.
1612	15. C (liveness): every party with a claim (refunder, winner, sponsorRecipient, treasury) can always eventually collect it; no reachable state strands USDC or the NFT for its rightful owner.
1613	
1614	## 5. Lifecycles (state touched per step)
1615	
1616	- **L1 Create**: `F:createRaffle` → `F:_validateCreateParams` (prize code, ERC-165, recipient screen, `reserveEntries>0`) → `Clones.clone` → `initialize` (sponsor, recipient, treasury, prize, id, reserve, endTime; `AwaitingPrize`) → `raffleById/idByRaffle/isRaffle` → `prize.safeTransferFrom` (untrusted code runs) → `onERC721Received` (`Active`) → `ownerOf` + `status` checks.
1617	- **L2 Sale** `[create, endTime)`: `buyEntries` → USDC in, `totalEntries`, `ticketCount`, `_ticketRanges`, `unsettledPot`, `_safeMint` (recipient code runs, `nonReentrant`).
1618	- **L3 Draw OK**: `requestDraw` (`Drawing`, `drawRequestedAt`, `_requestInFlight`, `vrfRequestId`, ETH out + excess refund call) → wrapper `rawFulfillRandomWords` → `fulfillRandomWords` (`winningEntry`, `resolvedAt`, `NftWon|CashWon`) → `settleWinningTicket` (split, `unsettledPot=0`) → `redeemWinningTicket` (burn; NFT or cash) → `releaseSponsorProceeds` / `releaseProtocolFees` → CashWon: `releaseSponsorPrize`.
1619	- **L4 Draw fails**: `requestDraw` → no / late / ignored callback → `enableRefunds` (Drawing branch, ≥ `callbackDeadline()`) → `refundTickets`×k → `releaseSponsorPrize`.
1620	- **L5 No draw**: sold raffle, nobody calls `requestDraw` in 2 days → `enableRefunds` (Active branch, ≥ `drawRequestDeadline()`) → refunds → prize back.
1621	- **L6 Empty**: `totalEntries==0` → sponsor `enableRefunds` any time, anyone after `endTime` → `releaseSponsorPrize`.
1622	- **L7 Ticket market**: transfer in any state via `_update` screen; whoever owns at redeem/refund time is paid; approved operators cannot redeem/refund (owner-only :321, :360).
1623	- **L8 Redeem-with-settle**: `redeemWinningTicket` on an unsettled raffle calls `_settleWinningTicket` itself :315.
1624	
1625	## 6. Cohorts (who is owed what)
1626	
1627	- **Sponsor** (`msg.sender` of `createRaffle`): escrows the NFT; may cancel an empty raffle early; may also buy entries (can move `totalEntries` across `reserveEntries`).
1628	- **sponsorRecipient** (immutable): `sponsorProceeds` + returned NFT.
1629	- **Protocol treasury** (factory immutable): 5% fee on any settled outcome; 0 on refunds.
1630	- **Buyers / ticket holders**: pay `n × 1e6`; owed 100% back in Refunding; otherwise only the winner is owed.
1631	- **Winner** = owner of the winning ticket at redemption: NFT (NftWon) or 80% of pot (CashWon). No redemption deadline.
1632	- **Last buyer before `endTime`**: knows `totalEntries` and decides whether the reserve is met.
1633	- **Draw requester** (anyone): pays the native VRF fee, never reimbursed. **Settler / releaser** (anyone): unpaid.
1634	- **Trusted**: USDC, Chainlink VRF v2.5 native wrapper. **Untrusted** (DESIGN.md): prize contract (gets control at F:128, F:129, :334-335, :404-405), ticket recipients (`_safeMint` :235, ticket `safeTransferFrom`), excess-ETH refund recipient :267.
1635	- **Not `nonReentrant`**: ERC-721 ticket `transferFrom/safeTransferFrom/approve/setApprovalForAll`, `onERC721Received`, `initialize`, `rawFulfillRandomWords`, views. Every other state-changing raffle function is `nonReentrant`; `F:createRaffle` is `nonReentrant` on the factory only.
1636	
1637	## 7. Timing table (exclusive upper bounds)
1638	
1639	| Action | Allowed when |
1640	| --- | --- |
1641	| `buyEntries` | `Active` and `now < endTime` :216 |
1642	| `requestDraw` | `Active`, `now >= endTime`, `totalEntries>0`, `now < endTime+2d` :241-247 |
1643	| callback resolves | `Drawing`, matching id, 1 word, not in-flight, `now < drawRequestedAt+2d` :510-513 |
1644	| `enableRefunds` | Active+sold: `now >= endTime+2d`; Drawing: `now >= drawRequestedAt+2d`; Active+empty: sponsor any time, others `now >= endTime` :279-294 |
1645	| settle / redeem | `NftWon` or `CashWon`, no deadline |
1646	| `releaseSponsorPrize` | `CashWon` or `Refunding`, once |
1647	# The 0xSimao Method
1648	
1649	Derived from 869 published findings across 143 reviews. This is HOW to think. Your lens file is WHAT to look for. Work them together.
1650	
1651	## The core thesis
1652	
1653	Most auditors read code looking for bad lines. That finds the bugs a linter finds.
1654	
1655	0xSimao reads code looking for **a claim that has drifted from what actually backs it**. Value moves through a protocol in sequences: deposit, accrue, borrow, liquidate, withdraw. Each step writes some subset of the accounting state, and drift is any way that state stops describing reality:
1656	
1657	| Drift | Shape |
1658	| --- | --- |
1659	| The write is missing | value moved and no variable recorded it — or one branch updates it and the sibling branch does not |
1660	| The write is wrong | the variable is updated with the wrong amount, direction, rounding, units, or decimals |
1661	| The write is mistimed | the right value at the wrong moment, so someone's snapshot is taken against state that is about to change |
1662	| The write goes to the wrong party | the total is intact; the split between cohorts is not |
1663	| The input was never trustworthy | the number is faithfully propagated from an oracle, a live balance, or a caller-supplied parameter an attacker controls |
1664	| The state is unreachable | the accounting is correct but a revert, a pause, an unbounded loop, or a missing path means it can never be settled |
1665	
1666	The drift is invisible at any single line. It only appears when you ask: *after this whole sequence, does the protocol still owe exactly what it holds — and can everyone actually collect it?*
1667	
1668	A defect nobody can be shown to lose money from is a curiosity. So every candidate gets one more question, and it is the one that separates a finding from a smell:
1669	
1670	> **Who is left holding the loss?**
1671	
1672	Answer with a named class of actor, never "users". For accounting drift it is often whoever withdraws last, because a shortfall stays invisible until the balance runs out — but for a bricked liquidation it is the solvent lenders eating the bad debt, for a mistimed snapshot it is the cohort that held through the accrual, and for a forged signature it is whoever the forged message was drawn against. If the only person worse off is the caller, there is no finding.
1673	
1674	**This lens is the sharpest one, not the only one.** Accounting drift is the largest single class in his corpus, but it is not the majority of it. The rest is DoS and permanently stuck funds, access control and signature defects, token- and integration-behaviour assumptions (`USDT` approvals, fee-on-transfer, blacklists, pausable collateral), oracle and parameter validation, and cross-chain state — and those are what your lens file owns. Work the money map first because it is what makes the drift class visible; then work your lens on its own terms. When the target has little accounting to speak of — a router, a registry, a verifier, a signature scheme — say so, keep the money map short, and go straight to your lens. Do not force a finding into the drift frame to make it sound like his.
1675	
1676	## Phase 0 — Learn the protocol's own vocabulary before reading for bugs
1677	
1678	His findings are written in the protocol's language: `cdsPoolValue`, `abond`, `downsideProtected`, `unassignedEarnings`, `raBalance`, `floatingBackupBorrowed`. He does not audit "a vault"; he audits *this* vault's specific accounting model.
1679	
1680	Before hunting, be able to state in plain English:
1681	- What does a user give, and what claim do they receive in return?
1682	- What is that claim worth, and which variables determine the value?
1683	- Where does yield come from, and who is entitled to it?
1684	- What happens when the protocol is short — who absorbs the shortfall?
1685	
1686	If you cannot answer these without Solidity jargon, you are not ready to find his class of bug. Any spot where your plain-English explanation goes fuzzy is exactly where the bug is; mark it and come back.
1687	
1688	## Phase 1 — Build the money map
1689	
1690	For every storage variable that claims to be an aggregate — `total*`, `*Supply`, `*Balance`, `*Deposited`, `*Locked`, `*Reserve`, `*Debt`, `*Accrued`, indices, cumulative rates — enumerate **every** function that writes it and whether that write increases or decreases it.
1691	
1692	Then build the asymmetry table. Three columns of pure gold:
1693	
1694	| Asymmetry | What to look for | Real finding |
1695	| --- | --- | --- |
1696	| Moved without tracking | value transferred out with no matching decrement | *"Users redeeming early will withdraw `Ra` without decreasing the amount locked, which will lead to stolen funds when withdrawing after expiry"* |
1697	| Tracked in one branch only | `if` updates the total, `else` does not | *"Users will steal excess funds from the Vault due to `VaultPoolLib::redeem()` not always decreasing `raBalance` and `paBalance`"* |
1698	| Never tracked at all | a balance is real but no variable represents it | *"Total `ETH`, `WETH` and `gameETH` are not tracked which will lead to insolvency"* |
1699	
1700	Also flag every place a **live balance read** (`token.balanceOf(address(this))`, `address(this).balance`) is used as an accounting source. That is a donation attack or a cross-user theft waiting to happen — *"`ManagedLeveragedVault::openDen()` using all `asset()` balance"*, *"SDAIPriceFeed is vulnerable to donation attack via manipulatable vault rate"*.
1701	
1702	## Phase 2 — Write the invariants down
1703	
1704	5–15 statements that must always hold. Concretely, not vaguely:
1705	
1706	- `Σ(all user withdrawable) <= actual token balance` — the solvency invariant, his single most productive one
1707	- `totalX == Σ userX` for every aggregate with a per-user counterpart
1708	- every credited unit is debited exactly once, in exactly one place
1709	- monotonic things (indices, cumulative rates, timestamps) never go backwards and cannot be advanced for free
1710	- a user's claim cannot increase from an action that costs them nothing
1711	- state on chain A and chain B agree after every message settles
1712	
1713	An invariant you can state and then break with a sequence is a finding. An invariant the docs assert and the code does not enforce is his highest-yield source of all.
1714	
1715	## Phase 3 — Run the lifecycles, not the functions
1716	
1717	Do not audit function by function. Audit *sequences*, and after each step write down which accounting variables changed and which should have.
1718	
1719	Canonical sequences to run:
1720	
1721	1. deposit → accrue yield → withdraw
1722	2. deposit → borrow → price moves → liquidate → withdraw
1723	3. stake → rewards distributed → unstake → claim
1724	4. deposit → withdraw → deposit again (re-entry into the same accounting slot — *"Borrower deposit, withdraw, deposit will reinit `omniChainData.cdsPoolValue`"*)
1725	5. open → adjust position → close (does the adjust path keep every invariant the open path established? — *"The health of a `ProtectedListing` is incorrectly calculated if `tokenTaken` has been changed through `adjustPosition()`"*)
1726	6. source chain send → destination chain receive → failure/retry
1727	7. the same sequence at expiry / after maturity / after the vault has ended
1728	
1729	For each, ask at every step: **what did we just change that something else still assumes the old value of?**
1730	
1731	## Phase 4 — Attack across cohorts and across time
1732	
1733	This is the most distinctive part of his method, and the least commonly imitated.
1734	
1735	Value in DeFi is split pro-rata among a changing set of holders. Any calculation that uses a *current* total to distribute a *historically accumulated* amount lets someone join late and take a share of value they did not earn.
1736	
1737	Three questions, applied to every distribution, reward, fee, yield, and profit path:
1738	
1739	1. **Can I join immediately before a distribution and take a share of it?**
1740	   *"Immediately start getting rewards belonging to others after staking"*, *"Late abond holders steal USDa amount from liquidations from earlier abond holders"*, *"increaseNetworkTotal() allows big arbitrage opportunities by depositing before an increase transaction"*
1741	2. **Can I leave immediately before a loss and push it onto whoever stays?**
1742	   *"Borrower withdrawing at a loss will cause losses for cds depositors that only withdraw after the price recovers"*
1743	3. **The Last User Out test.** Have every user withdraw, in sequence, in the worst order. Does the last one get paid? If the protocol is short by even dust, the money map has a leak upstream — go find it.
1744	   *"`totalEarnings` is incorrect when withdrawing after ending which will withdraw too many funds leaving the `Vault` insolvent"*
1745	
1746	Cumulative-rate and index-based accounting deserves special hostility: check whether the index can be advanced without cost (*"Malicious user can call `calculateCumulativeRate()` any number of times to inflate debt rate as `lastEventTime` is not updated"*), and whether a user's snapshot is taken at the right moment (*"Depositing to another receiver other than `msg.sender` will lead to stuck funds by increasing `avgStart` without claiming"*).
1747	
1748	## Phase 5 — Saturate the subsystem
1749	
1750	When you find one bug, **do not move on**. His reports cluster: 38 findings in one protocol, most in a single accounting subsystem. That is not luck. Once the accounting model is in your head, mine it out.
1751	
1752	After every finding:
1753	1. Search the codebase for every other site with the same code shape — by function name *and* by pattern. If `redeem()` forgets a decrement, check `withdraw()`, `emergencyWithdraw()`, `redeemExpired()`, and the cross-chain variant.
1754	2. Attack the other branches of the function where you found it.
1755	3. Escalate: a DoS often conceals fund theft; a rounding error often compounds into drain. Push each finding to its worst exploitable variant before writing it up.
1756	
1757	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure, not an omission.
1758	
1759	## Phase 6 — Prove it, with preconditions stated honestly
1760	
1761	His writeups make the reader's job trivial by separating what the protocol must look like from what the world must look like:
1762	
1763	- **Internal pre-conditions** — protocol state required (a maturity exists, a position is near liquidation, deposits are non-zero). "None" is common and is the strongest possible case.
1764	- **External pre-conditions** — market/oracle/chain conditions required (price moves X%, sequencer down, gas above Y). "None" is again the strongest case.
1765	- **Attack path** — numbered, concrete, with actors and numbers. Not "an attacker could manipulate the rate" but "1. User deposits 100e18. 2. User is liquidated via `liquidationType1()`, adding 5e18 USDa. 3. Attacker deposits via flashloan and withdraws, taking 4.9e18 of it."
1766	- **Impact** — who loses what. Name the victim class.
1767	
1768	If you cannot fill the attack path with real numbers, you have a LEAD. Say so. A well-described lead is worth more than a finding you inflated.
1769	
1770	## Phase 7 — Minimal mitigation
1771	
1772	One change, the smallest that removes the defect, stated in the protocol's own terms:
1773	
1774	- "Add a cumulative tracking variable to handle this case."
1775	- "Set the vesting interest to 0 when the new interest is 0."
1776	- "Decrease `raBalance` in the early-redemption branch as well."
1777	- "Use `mulDiv` when converting between token and share amounts."
1778	
1779	Not "refactor the accounting system." Not "consider adding validation." Name the operation to add, remove, or reorder.
1780	
1781	## Three habits that separate his findings from noise
1782	
1783	**Root cause is a missing operation at a named line.** Very often the bug is not a wrong line but an absent one. Write it that way: *"In `PsmLib.sol:125`, `self.psm.balances.ra.decLocked(amount)` is not called."* Pointing at the absence is what makes the fix obvious.
1784	
1785	**Judge what the code allows, never what the deployer intends.** "The admin wouldn't do that" is not a mitigation. But equally, "admin can rug" with no concrete mechanism is not a finding.
1786	
1787	**Doubt the clean-looking path hardest.** The functions that read as obviously correct are the ones everyone else also skipped. When a guard looks sufficient, name three specific ways to defeat it — with addresses, values, and states, not abstractions — before you accept it.
1788	
1789	## Do not report
1790	
1791	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Standard, accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a swap the user chose, rounding dust with no amplification, first-depositor inflation where `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` or a virtual-share offset is already present). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" with no mechanism. Gas optimizations dressed as vulnerabilities. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters.
1792	# Lens 7 — Ordering, MEV & Price Manipulation
1793	
1794	You own everything that depends on *when* a transaction lands relative to others: frontrunning, sandwiching, initialization races, oracle reads, and arbitrage against discrete state changes.
1795	
1796	The bar matters here. Ordinary slippage on a swap a user chose is not a finding. What you are hunting is (a) protocol-owned value exposed to MEV without protection, (b) a state change large enough to arbitrage, and (c) a one-shot action anyone can win.
1797	
1798	## Attack surfaces
1799	
1800	**Win the initialization race.** Any `initialize`, first-deposit, pool-creation, or set-once function callable by anyone before the deployer gets there. These are consistently High: an arbitrary initial price or an attacker-owned proxy is total loss.
1801	> *Uniswap v4 pool initialization can be frontrunned, setting an arbitrary price, and stealing tokens*
1802	> *`BoldToken` initialization can be frontrun to silently mint/approve bold to an attacker*
1803	> *Missing `__Ownable_init()` call in `LenderCommitmentGroup_Smart::initialize()`*
1804	> *`Codeup::claimCodeupERC20()` may be forever DoSed by creating the `Uniswap` pool before it is called*
1805	
1806	**Find protocol-owned swaps with no protection.** A permissionless function that swaps protocol funds with `amountOutMin = 0` or `deadline = block.timestamp` is free money for a sandwicher, and the protocol — not a consenting user — pays.
1807	> *Distribute is permissionless, allowing malicious users to specify 0 slippage and sandwich the swap*
1808	> *Swapping with deadline as `block.timestamp` and 0 minimum amount out is vulnerable to MEV*
1809	> *`UniswapV2Swapper` uses `block.timestamp` for deadline*
1810	> *`_addLiquidity()` slippage is incorrectly set*
1811	> *Lack of deadline in `PowerToken.buy` can lead to user's cashToken being distributed through ZeroToken holders*
1812	
1813	**Arbitrage the discrete jump.** Any transaction that steps a rate, TVL, price, or reserve discontinuously can be front-run on one side and back-run on the other. Look for admin rate updates, reward top-ups, rebalances, and TVL syncs.
1814	> *`increaseNetworkTotal()` allows big arbitrage opportunities by depositing before an increase transaction*
1815	> *Withdrawals logic allows MEV exploits of TVL changes and zero-slippage zero-fee swaps*
1816	> *`_rebalanceWithdraw()` mechanism in glAVAX allows arbitrage opportunities by changing the shares/AVAX ratio*
1817	> *Price formula in `TpdaLiquidationPair._computePrice()` does not account for a jump in liquidatable balance*
1818	> *Drained oracle fees from market by depositing and withdrawing immediately without triggering settlement fees*
1819	
1820	**Read the manipulable price.** `slot0`, spot reserves, and any vault rate derived from a live balance are manipulable within a single transaction. Distinguish a genuine TWAP from a spot read dressed as one, and check which price the protocol picks when several are available.
1821	> *Strategy main ticks are set according to the tick in `slot0`, leading to incorrect allocation and loss of funds*
1822	> *`LenderCommitmentGroup_Smart` picks the wrong Uniswap price, allowing borrowing at a discount by swapping before withdrawing*
1823	> *Interest rate in `LenderCommitmentGroup_Smart` may be easily manipulated by depositing, taking a loan and withdrawing*
1824	> *`PHyperLPoolSwapInside::_rebalance()` checks the price manipulation before and after the swap with the same price threshold*
1825	> *Locker owners can leverage low liquidity pools to bypass the tax mechanism*
1826	
1827	**Front-run for grief, not profit.** Cancelling a raffle before it starts, claiming a one-shot right, resetting someone's timer, or triggering a state transition to block another user. Cost to the attacker is often near zero.
1828	> *Attacker will prevent any raffles by calling `WinnablesTicketManager::cancelRaffle` before admin starts raffle*
1829	> *Malicious user may frontrun `GoodDollarExpansionController::mintUBIFromReserveBalance()` to make protocol funds stuck*
1830	> *Anyone can frontrun a relayer interaction with the same arguments but a much higher/lower relayer fee*
1831	> *Anyone will DoS setting a new rewards duration which harms the protocol/users*
1832	
1833	**Break the approval window.** Functions taking shares (rather than assets) as an argument, or relying on a prior approval, can be made to revert or over-spend if state moves between approval and execution.
1834	> *`repay()`, `liquidate()` and `liquidateWLp()` receive shares as argument, which may revert if from approval to tx settled blocks have passed*
1835	> *`safeApprove(...)` reverts if approval is different than 0, use `safeIncreaseAllowance(...)` instead*
1836	> *`FlashRolloverLoan_G5` will not work for certain tokens due to not setting the approval to `0` after repaying a loan*
1837	
1838	**Replay the signature.** Missing nonce, missing deadline, missing chain id, zero timestamp accepted, or parameters excluded from the signed digest so an attacker can pair a valid signature with hostile arguments.
1839	> *Validator signature with zero timestamp can always be replayed*
1840	> *Signature Replay attack possible on `updateWorkerDeploymentConfigWithSig()` in Blueprintcore.sol which leads to users losing funds*
1841	> *Signatures missing some parameters being vulnerable to attackers using them coupled with malicious parameters*
1842	> *All curve params should be signed by the schnorr private key in the proof, or users may be griefed*
1843	
1844	## Every finding needs the ordering
1845	
1846	State the transaction sequence explicitly: attacker tx, victim tx, attacker tx. Give the attacker's cost and profit. If the attack is a grief, state the cost to the attacker (often zero) and the damage to the victim.
1847	# Shared Lens Rules
1848	
1849	## Bundle contents
1850	
1851	Your bundle is five concatenated parts: all in-scope source, the protocol's **money map** (built by the orchestrator), the **method** (how to think), your **lens** (what you own), and these shared rules (output format and protocol).
1852	
1853	Read the whole bundle once at the start. Do not re-read in-scope files for the initial scan. Read or search the repo only for cross-file lookups or out-of-scope context (`interfaces/`, `lib/`, `mocks/`, `test/`).
1854	
1855	**Start from the money map, not the file list.** Pick the tracked totals, lifecycles, and cohorts your lens owns, and attack those. The file list is where you go to confirm, not where you begin.
1856	
1857	When matching function names, check both `functionName` and `_functionName` (Solidity convention), and check library variants (`XLib::function`).
1858	
1859	## Public audit-evidence summaries
1860	
1861	Provide concise public audit evidence and final conclusions, with source references. Do not provide private working text, hidden chain-of-thought, or a transcript of internal deliberation. The following labels organize the public report; they are not instructions to reveal private reasoning or to emit intermediate working text before continuing.
1862	
1863	| Evidence category | Public label | Brief report content |
1864	| --- | --- | --- |
1865	| A function moves value or writes a tracked total | `[Model: <name>]` | Summarize what a user gives, what they receive, and the totals changed, citing the relevant function. |
1866	| A non-obvious operation relies on an assumption | `[Why: <file:line>]` | State the relevant assumption and the source evidence establishing it, or identify the unresolved assumption. |
1867	| An access guard or value-moving path is assessed | `[Defeat: <function>]` | Report concise boundary-test or adversarial-case outcomes and the effective guard or uncovered condition; no private deliberation is requested. |
1868	| A lifecycle is assessed | `[LastOut: <lifecycle>]` | State the conservation/liability result and whether all eligible users can receive the amounts owed, with evidence or a clearly identified gap. |
1869	
1870	Use these summaries as public evidence for the audit result. The orchestrator may inventory which evidence categories were covered; it must not request or evaluate private reasoning traces. All remaining lens scope, saturation, finding format, severity, adjudication, proof and reporting rules are unchanged.
1871	
1872	## Saturation is mandatory
1873	
1874	When you find a bug, weaponize the pattern across the entire codebase before moving on. Search by function name AND by code shape. If one redemption path forgets a decrement, check every other redemption, withdrawal, emergency, expiry, and cross-chain variant. Then attack the other branches of the function where you found it. Then escalate the finding to its worst exploitable variant — a DoS often hides fund theft.
1875	
1876	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure.
1877	
1878	## Do not report
1879	
1880	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a user-chosen swap, rounding dust with no amplification path, first-depositor inflation where a virtual-share offset or `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` already exists). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" or "admin can rug" without a concrete mechanism. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters. Gas findings.
1881	
1882	## Output
1883	
1884	FINDINGs have a concrete, unguarded, exploitable path with a named victim. LEADs have a real accounting or logic smell with a partial path. Default to LEAD over dropping — never drop.
1885	
1886	**One vulnerability per block.** Same root cause = one block. Needs a different fix = separate block.
1887	
1888	```
1889	FINDING | contract: Name | function: func | bug_class: kebab-tag | group_key: Contract | function | bug-class
1890	root_cause: the defect at File.sol:LINE, naming the missing or wrong operation
1891	internal_pre: protocol state required, or None
1892	external_pre: market/oracle/chain conditions required, or None
1893	path:
1894	  1. actor does X with concrete amount
1895	  2. state changes to Y
1896	  3. actor does Z
1897	impact: who loses what, and who is left holding the loss
1898	mitigation: the single smallest change that removes the defect
1899	```
1900	
1901	```
1902	LEAD | contract: Name | function: func | bug_class: kebab-tag | group_key: Contract | function | bug-class
1903	smell: what you found
1904	unverified: precisely what you could not establish
1905	description: one sentence on the trail
1906	```
1907	
1908	`group_key` drives deduplication and is always `ContractName | functionName | bug_class`.
1909	
1910	An `internal_pre` or `external_pre` of `None` is the strongest possible finding — never pad these to look thorough. State the truth.

1543	# Clean design specification
1544	Ethereum NFT raffle; immutable factory, ERC-1167 clones with immutable implementation. One entry costs 1,000,000 units of canonical six-decimal USDC. One purchase mints a transferable ERC721 ticket representing a contiguous inclusive range. Exactly one ERC721 prize is escrowed atomically at creation. Reserve met awards NFT and 95% sponsor / 5% treasury. Reserve missed awards 80% gross to winner, 15% sponsor, 5% treasury. Refund outcome pays 100% per entry and returns prize. Rounding is floor on aggregate protocol fee; remainder must be allocated without loss. No administrator, mutable configuration or upgrade. Request window [sale end, end+2days); callback accepted strictly before request timestamp+2days. Refunds open at deadline. Callback records result only. Settlement is permissionless, storage-only; redemption requires current ticket owner, burns claim atomically, and must revert all effects on delivery failure. Sponsor and treasury can claim independently after settlement. Never move assets between raffle clones. Quote token and Chainlink wrapper are trusted canonical dependencies; arbitrary prize contracts and ticket recipients are untrusted. Frontend discovery is advisory; transaction decisions must reread current chain state.
1545	
1546	This specification was composed before scanner results and historical findings. Source, not design prose, determines actual behavior. No tests, audit history, accepted-risk lists or scanner results are provided.

1647	# The 0xSimao Method
1648	
1649	Derived from 869 published findings across 143 reviews. This is HOW to think. Your lens file is WHAT to look for. Work them together.
1650	
1651	## The core thesis
1652	
1653	Most auditors read code looking for bad lines. That finds the bugs a linter finds.
1654	
1655	0xSimao reads code looking for **a claim that has drifted from what actually backs it**. Value moves through a protocol in sequences: deposit, accrue, borrow, liquidate, withdraw. Each step writes some subset of the accounting state, and drift is any way that state stops describing reality:
1656	
1657	| Drift | Shape |
1658	| --- | --- |
1659	| The write is missing | value moved and no variable recorded it — or one branch updates it and the sibling branch does not |
1660	| The write is wrong | the variable is updated with the wrong amount, direction, rounding, units, or decimals |
1661	| The write is mistimed | the right value at the wrong moment, so someone's snapshot is taken against state that is about to change |
1662	| The write goes to the wrong party | the total is intact; the split between cohorts is not |
1663	| The input was never trustworthy | the number is faithfully propagated from an oracle, a live balance, or a caller-supplied parameter an attacker controls |
1664	| The state is unreachable | the accounting is correct but a revert, a pause, an unbounded loop, or a missing path means it can never be settled |
1665	
1666	The drift is invisible at any single line. It only appears when you ask: *after this whole sequence, does the protocol still owe exactly what it holds — and can everyone actually collect it?*
1667	
1668	A defect nobody can be shown to lose money from is a curiosity. So every candidate gets one more question, and it is the one that separates a finding from a smell:
1669	
1670	> **Who is left holding the loss?**
1671	
1672	Answer with a named class of actor, never "users". For accounting drift it is often whoever withdraws last, because a shortfall stays invisible until the balance runs out — but for a bricked liquidation it is the solvent lenders eating the bad debt, for a mistimed snapshot it is the cohort that held through the accrual, and for a forged signature it is whoever the forged message was drawn against. If the only person worse off is the caller, there is no finding.
1673	
1674	**This lens is the sharpest one, not the only one.** Accounting drift is the largest single class in his corpus, but it is not the majority of it. The rest is DoS and permanently stuck funds, access control and signature defects, token- and integration-behaviour assumptions (`USDT` approvals, fee-on-transfer, blacklists, pausable collateral), oracle and parameter validation, and cross-chain state — and those are what your lens file owns. Work the money map first because it is what makes the drift class visible; then work your lens on its own terms. When the target has little accounting to speak of — a router, a registry, a verifier, a signature scheme — say so, keep the money map short, and go straight to your lens. Do not force a finding into the drift frame to make it sound like his.
1675	
1676	## Phase 0 — Learn the protocol's own vocabulary before reading for bugs
1677	
1678	His findings are written in the protocol's language: `cdsPoolValue`, `abond`, `downsideProtected`, `unassignedEarnings`, `raBalance`, `floatingBackupBorrowed`. He does not audit "a vault"; he audits *this* vault's specific accounting model.
1679	
1680	Before hunting, be able to state in plain English:
1681	- What does a user give, and what claim do they receive in return?
1682	- What is that claim worth, and which variables determine the value?
1683	- Where does yield come from, and who is entitled to it?
1684	- What happens when the protocol is short — who absorbs the shortfall?
1685	
1686	If you cannot answer these without Solidity jargon, you are not ready to find his class of bug. Any spot where your plain-English explanation goes fuzzy is exactly where the bug is; mark it and come back.
1687	
1688	## Phase 1 — Build the money map
1689	
1690	For every storage variable that claims to be an aggregate — `total*`, `*Supply`, `*Balance`, `*Deposited`, `*Locked`, `*Reserve`, `*Debt`, `*Accrued`, indices, cumulative rates — enumerate **every** function that writes it and whether that write increases or decreases it.
1691	
1692	Then build the asymmetry table. Three columns of pure gold:
1693	
1694	| Asymmetry | What to look for | Real finding |
1695	| --- | --- | --- |
1696	| Moved without tracking | value transferred out with no matching decrement | *"Users redeeming early will withdraw `Ra` without decreasing the amount locked, which will lead to stolen funds when withdrawing after expiry"* |
1697	| Tracked in one branch only | `if` updates the total, `else` does not | *"Users will steal excess funds from the Vault due to `VaultPoolLib::redeem()` not always decreasing `raBalance` and `paBalance`"* |
1698	| Never tracked at all | a balance is real but no variable represents it | *"Total `ETH`, `WETH` and `gameETH` are not tracked which will lead to insolvency"* |
1699	
1700	Also flag every place a **live balance read** (`token.balanceOf(address(this))`, `address(this).balance`) is used as an accounting source. That is a donation attack or a cross-user theft waiting to happen — *"`ManagedLeveragedVault::openDen()` using all `asset()` balance"*, *"SDAIPriceFeed is vulnerable to donation attack via manipulatable vault rate"*.
1701	
1702	## Phase 2 — Write the invariants down
1703	
1704	5–15 statements that must always hold. Concretely, not vaguely:
1705	
1706	- `Σ(all user withdrawable) <= actual token balance` — the solvency invariant, his single most productive one
1707	- `totalX == Σ userX` for every aggregate with a per-user counterpart
1708	- every credited unit is debited exactly once, in exactly one place
1709	- monotonic things (indices, cumulative rates, timestamps) never go backwards and cannot be advanced for free
1710	- a user's claim cannot increase from an action that costs them nothing
1711	- state on chain A and chain B agree after every message settles
1712	
1713	An invariant you can state and then break with a sequence is a finding. An invariant the docs assert and the code does not enforce is his highest-yield source of all.
1714	
1715	## Phase 3 — Run the lifecycles, not the functions
1716	
1717	Do not audit function by function. Audit *sequences*, and after each step write down which accounting variables changed and which should have.
1718	
1719	Canonical sequences to run:
1720	
1721	1. deposit → accrue yield → withdraw
1722	2. deposit → borrow → price moves → liquidate → withdraw
1723	3. stake → rewards distributed → unstake → claim
1724	4. deposit → withdraw → deposit again (re-entry into the same accounting slot — *"Borrower deposit, withdraw, deposit will reinit `omniChainData.cdsPoolValue`"*)
1725	5. open → adjust position → close (does the adjust path keep every invariant the open path established? — *"The health of a `ProtectedListing` is incorrectly calculated if `tokenTaken` has been changed through `adjustPosition()`"*)
1726	6. source chain send → destination chain receive → failure/retry
1727	7. the same sequence at expiry / after maturity / after the vault has ended
1728	
1729	For each, ask at every step: **what did we just change that something else still assumes the old value of?**
1730	
1731	## Phase 4 — Attack across cohorts and across time
1732	
1733	This is the most distinctive part of his method, and the least commonly imitated.
1734	
1735	Value in DeFi is split pro-rata among a changing set of holders. Any calculation that uses a *current* total to distribute a *historically accumulated* amount lets someone join late and take a share of value they did not earn.
1736	
1737	Three questions, applied to every distribution, reward, fee, yield, and profit path:
1738	
1739	1. **Can I join immediately before a distribution and take a share of it?**
1740	   *"Immediately start getting rewards belonging to others after staking"*, *"Late abond holders steal USDa amount from liquidations from earlier abond holders"*, *"increaseNetworkTotal() allows big arbitrage opportunities by depositing before an increase transaction"*
1741	2. **Can I leave immediately before a loss and push it onto whoever stays?**
1742	   *"Borrower withdrawing at a loss will cause losses for cds depositors that only withdraw after the price recovers"*
1743	3. **The Last User Out test.** Have every user withdraw, in sequence, in the worst order. Does the last one get paid? If the protocol is short by even dust, the money map has a leak upstream — go find it.
1744	   *"`totalEarnings` is incorrect when withdrawing after ending which will withdraw too many funds leaving the `Vault` insolvent"*
1745	
1746	Cumulative-rate and index-based accounting deserves special hostility: check whether the index can be advanced without cost (*"Malicious user can call `calculateCumulativeRate()` any number of times to inflate debt rate as `lastEventTime` is not updated"*), and whether a user's snapshot is taken at the right moment (*"Depositing to another receiver other than `msg.sender` will lead to stuck funds by increasing `avgStart` without claiming"*).
1747	
1748	## Phase 5 — Saturate the subsystem
1749	
1750	When you find one bug, **do not move on**. His reports cluster: 38 findings in one protocol, most in a single accounting subsystem. That is not luck. Once the accounting model is in your head, mine it out.
1751	
1752	After every finding:
1753	1. Search the codebase for every other site with the same code shape — by function name *and* by pattern. If `redeem()` forgets a decrement, check `withdraw()`, `emergencyWithdraw()`, `redeemExpired()`, and the cross-chain variant.
1754	2. Attack the other branches of the function where you found it.
1755	3. Escalate: a DoS often conceals fund theft; a rounding error often compounds into drain. Push each finding to its worst exploitable variant before writing it up.
1756	
1757	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure, not an omission.
1758	
1759	## Phase 6 — Prove it, with preconditions stated honestly
1760	
1761	His writeups make the reader's job trivial by separating what the protocol must look like from what the world must look like:
1762	
1763	- **Internal pre-conditions** — protocol state required (a maturity exists, a position is near liquidation, deposits are non-zero). "None" is common and is the strongest possible case.
1764	- **External pre-conditions** — market/oracle/chain conditions required (price moves X%, sequencer down, gas above Y). "None" is again the strongest case.
1765	- **Attack path** — numbered, concrete, with actors and numbers. Not "an attacker could manipulate the rate" but "1. User deposits 100e18. 2. User is liquidated via `liquidationType1()`, adding 5e18 USDa. 3. Attacker deposits via flashloan and withdraws, taking 4.9e18 of it."
1766	- **Impact** — who loses what. Name the victim class.
1767	
1768	If you cannot fill the attack path with real numbers, you have a LEAD. Say so. A well-described lead is worth more than a finding you inflated.
1769	
1770	## Phase 7 — Minimal mitigation
1771	
1772	One change, the smallest that removes the defect, stated in the protocol's own terms:
1773	
1774	- "Add a cumulative tracking variable to handle this case."
1775	- "Set the vesting interest to 0 when the new interest is 0."
1776	- "Decrease `raBalance` in the early-redemption branch as well."
1777	- "Use `mulDiv` when converting between token and share amounts."
1778	
1779	Not "refactor the accounting system." Not "consider adding validation." Name the operation to add, remove, or reorder.
1780	
1781	## Three habits that separate his findings from noise
1782	
1783	**Root cause is a missing operation at a named line.** Very often the bug is not a wrong line but an absent one. Write it that way: *"In `PsmLib.sol:125`, `self.psm.balances.ra.decLocked(amount)` is not called."* Pointing at the absence is what makes the fix obvious.
1784	
1785	**Judge what the code allows, never what the deployer intends.** "The admin wouldn't do that" is not a mitigation. But equally, "admin can rug" with no concrete mechanism is not a finding.
1786	
1787	**Doubt the clean-looking path hardest.** The functions that read as obviously correct are the ones everyone else also skipped. When a guard looks sufficient, name three specific ways to defeat it — with addresses, values, and states, not abstractions — before you accept it.
1788	
1789	## Do not report
1790	
1791	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Standard, accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a swap the user chose, rounding dust with no amplification, first-depositor inflation where `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` or a virtual-share offset is already present). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" with no mechanism. Gas optimizations dressed as vulnerabilities. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters.
1792	# Lens 8 — Denial of Service & Griefing
1793	
1794	You own availability. Your target is not "this could revert" — it is **a permanent or long-lived block on a function that must remain available, reachable by an attacker at low cost, with a real cost to someone else.**
1795	
1796	The severity ladder that matters: funds permanently stuck > liquidations blocked (because bad debt accrues) > withdrawals blocked for a bounded period > core function unusable > admin function unusable.
1797	
1798	## Attack surfaces
1799	
1800	**Grow an unbounded array.** Any loop over a user-extendable structure — queues, pending removals, request lists, holder arrays, market lists — is an out-of-gas bomb if anyone can append cheaply. Ask for the batch parameter; note its absence.
1801	> *DoSed `Voter::finalize()` due to unbounded pending removals lacking a batch argument variable*
1802	> *`BatchOut::withdrawFulfill()` can be DoSed by spamming withdrawal requests, leading to OOG reverts*
1803	> *`Treasury.noOfBorrowers` can be set to 0 by looping wei deposit<->withdrawals and DoS withdrawals and reset borrower debt*
1804	
1805	**Poison one element of a batch.** A single reverting item in a loop that reverts the whole transaction. Reverting hooks, blacklisted recipients, zero-transfer-reverting tokens, and `address(0)` entries are all cheap to inject.
1806	> *Halted withdrawals in BatchOut due to setting `withdrawTo` to `address(0)` in `scheduleWithdrawal()`*
1807	> *Scheduled withdrawals with unsupported tokens will be halted*
1808	> *`Claimers` can receive less `feePerClaim` than they should if some prizes are already claimed or if reverts because of a reverting hook*
1809	> *If wLP is blacklisted, then user will not be able to withdraw it*
1810	> *Gas Manipulation by Malicious Winners in `claimPrizes` Function*
1811	
1812	**Exhaust a shared resource.** Buffers, caps, queues, and limits that any user can fill to lock everyone else out.
1813	> *DOS of `completeQueuedWithdrawal` when ERC20 buffer is filled*
1814	> *Attacker can DoS user withdrawals at no cost*
1815	> *Anyone can grief users, stopping them from fulfilling their withdrawals*
1816	> *Worker-Induced Denial-of-Service in Deployment Requests Due to Lack of a Cancellation Mechanism*
1817	
1818	**Make the internal call impossible.** A function that internally deposits, withdraws, harvests, or rebalances will inherit every failure mode of the thing it calls. Full utilization, paused markets, frozen assets, and reverting receive hooks all propagate up into a core path that looks unrelated.
1819	> *Market utilization ratio near 100% will DoS deposits as harvest tries to withdraw and reverts*
1820	> *Frozen/paused Market that is harvested from in StakedEXA will DoS deposits leading to loss of yield*
1821	> *Setting a new market will make depositing to the market impossible when harvesting, DoSing deposits*
1822	> *Withdrawals can fail due to deposits reverting in `completeQueuedWithdrawal()`*
1823	> *ETH withdrawals from EigenLayer always fail due to `OperatorDelegator`'s nonReentrant `receive()`*
1824	
1825	**Interrogate the pause switches.** Pausing is meant to be selective and reversible. Check that pausing one thing does not block another that must stay live (repay, liquidate, withdraw), that the pause can actually be applied as documented, and that unpausing restores state.
1826	> *Cannot repay or liquidate on paused asset*
1827	> *Admin will not be able to only pause deposits in the `Vault` due to incorrect check leading to DoSed withdrawals*
1828	> *Withdrawals and Claims are meant to be pausable, but it is not possible in practice*
1829	> *`SpiritFactory` won't be able to stop the Airstream contract*
1830	
1831	**Brick the upgrade or the config.** Permanent loss of administrative control is a real finding when it makes the contract unfixable.
1832	> *Admin will not be able to upgrade the smart contracts, breaking core functionality and rendering the upgradeable contracts useless*
1833	> *FeeManager's admin cannot grant or revoke any role*
1834	> *Incompatibility of Upgradeability Pattern in TitlesGraph Contract*
1835	> *Changing the epoch duration will completely break the vault and the slashers*
1836	
1837	**Trap value with a state machine.** A state that cannot be exited, a request that cannot be cancelled, a flag that cannot be cleared, a threshold that can never be met.
1838	> *`FluidLocker::_getUnlockingPercentage()` uses 540 instead of `540 days` leading to stuck funds*
1839	> *It's impossible to retrieve collected fines from the yield staking contract*
1840	> *Unhandled request invalidation by the owner of Etherfi will lead to stuck debt*
1841	> *Users cannot unstake from YiedlETHStakingEtherfi.sol, because YieldAccount.sol is incompatible with ether.fi's WithdrawRequestNFT.sol*
1842	> *Aura/Convex rewards are stuck after DOS*
1843	
1844	**Overwrite index zero.** Sentinel-value bugs where "not found" returns 0 and the caller writes to slot 0, destroying a real entry.
1845	> *In OstiumTradingStorage, `firstEmptyTradeIndex()` and `firstEmptyOpenLimitIndex()` overwrite index 0 if not found*
1846	
1847	## Escalate before reporting
1848	
1849	A DoS very often conceals a theft: while withdrawals are blocked, does the rate drift? Can the attacker withdraw during the window? Does the blocked liquidation let them keep an underwater position? Push every DoS to its worst variant before writing it up.
1850	
1851	## Every finding needs the cost
1852	
1853	State the attacker's cost (gas, capital, whether the capital is recoverable), the duration of the block (permanent vs bounded — say which), and who cannot do what. A DoS an attacker cannot afford to sustain is a LEAD.
1854	# Shared Lens Rules
1855	
1856	## Bundle contents
1857	
1858	Your bundle is five concatenated parts: all in-scope source, the protocol's **money map** (built by the orchestrator), the **method** (how to think), your **lens** (what you own), and these shared rules (output format and protocol).
1859	
1860	Read the whole bundle once at the start. Do not re-read in-scope files for the initial scan. Read or search the repo only for cross-file lookups or out-of-scope context (`interfaces/`, `lib/`, `mocks/`, `test/`).
1861	
1862	**Start from the money map, not the file list.** Pick the tracked totals, lifecycles, and cohorts your lens owns, and attack those. The file list is where you go to confirm, not where you begin.
1863	
1864	When matching function names, check both `functionName` and `_functionName` (Solidity convention), and check library variants (`XLib::function`).
1865	
1866	## Public audit-evidence summaries
1867	
1868	Provide concise public audit evidence and final conclusions, with source references. Do not provide private working text, hidden chain-of-thought, or a transcript of internal deliberation. The following labels organize the public report; they are not instructions to reveal private reasoning or to emit intermediate working text before continuing.
1869	
1870	| Evidence category | Public label | Brief report content |
1871	| --- | --- | --- |
1872	| A function moves value or writes a tracked total | `[Model: <name>]` | Summarize what a user gives, what they receive, and the totals changed, citing the relevant function. |
1873	| A non-obvious operation relies on an assumption | `[Why: <file:line>]` | State the relevant assumption and the source evidence establishing it, or identify the unresolved assumption. |
1874	| An access guard or value-moving path is assessed | `[Defeat: <function>]` | Report concise boundary-test or adversarial-case outcomes and the effective guard or uncovered condition; no private deliberation is requested. |
1875	| A lifecycle is assessed | `[LastOut: <lifecycle>]` | State the conservation/liability result and whether all eligible users can receive the amounts owed, with evidence or a clearly identified gap. |
1876	
1877	Use these summaries as public evidence for the audit result. The orchestrator may inventory which evidence categories were covered; it must not request or evaluate private reasoning traces. All remaining lens scope, saturation, finding format, severity, adjudication, proof and reporting rules are unchanged.
1878	
1879	## Saturation is mandatory
1880	
1881	When you find a bug, weaponize the pattern across the entire codebase before moving on. Search by function name AND by code shape. If one redemption path forgets a decrement, check every other redemption, withdrawal, emergency, expiry, and cross-chain variant. Then attack the other branches of the function where you found it. Then escalate the finding to its worst exploitable variant — a DoS often hides fund theft.
1882	
1883	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure.
1884	
1885	## Do not report
1886	
1887	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a user-chosen swap, rounding dust with no amplification path, first-depositor inflation where a virtual-share offset or `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` already exists). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" or "admin can rug" without a concrete mechanism. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters. Gas findings.
1888	
1889	## Output
1890	
1891	FINDINGs have a concrete, unguarded, exploitable path with a named victim. LEADs have a real accounting or logic smell with a partial path. Default to LEAD over dropping — never drop.
1892	
1893	**One vulnerability per block.** Same root cause = one block. Needs a different fix = separate block.
1894	
1895	```
1896	FINDING | contract: Name | function: func | bug_class: kebab-tag | group_key: Contract | function | bug-class
1897	root_cause: the defect at File.sol:LINE, naming the missing or wrong operation
1898	internal_pre: protocol state required, or None
1899	external_pre: market/oracle/chain conditions required, or None
1900	path:
1901	  1. actor does X with concrete amount
1902	  2. state changes to Y
1903	  3. actor does Z
1904	impact: who loses what, and who is left holding the loss
1905	mitigation: the single smallest change that removes the defect
1906	```
1907	
1908	```
1909	LEAD | contract: Name | function: func | bug_class: kebab-tag | group_key: Contract | function | bug-class
1910	smell: what you found
1911	unverified: precisely what you could not establish
1912	description: one sentence on the trail
1913	```
1914	
1915	`group_key` drives deduplication and is always `ContractName | functionName | bug_class`.
1916	
1917	An `internal_pre` or `external_pre` of `None` is the strongest possible finding — never pad these to look thorough. State the truth.

1542	```markdown
1543	# Clean design specification
1544	Ethereum NFT raffle; immutable factory, ERC-1167 clones with immutable implementation. One entry costs 1,000,000 units of canonical six-decimal USDC. One purchase mints a transferable ERC721 ticket representing a contiguous inclusive range. Exactly one ERC721 prize is escrowed atomically at creation. Reserve met awards NFT and 95% sponsor / 5% treasury. Reserve missed awards 80% gross to winner, 15% sponsor, 5% treasury. Refund outcome pays 100% per entry and returns prize. Rounding is floor on aggregate protocol fee; remainder must be allocated without loss. No administrator, mutable configuration or upgrade. Request window [sale end, end+2days); callback accepted strictly before request timestamp+2days. Refunds open at deadline. Callback records result only. Settlement is permissionless, storage-only; redemption requires current ticket owner, burns claim atomically, and must revert all effects on delivery failure. Sponsor and treasury can claim independently after settlement. Never move assets between raffle clones. Quote token and Chainlink wrapper are trusted canonical dependencies; arbitrary prize contracts and ticket recipients are untrusted. Frontend discovery is advisory; transaction decisions must reread current chain state.
1545	
1546	This specification was composed before scanner results and historical findings. Source, not design prose, determines actual behavior. No tests, audit history, accepted-risk lists or scanner results are provided.
1547	```

1647	# The 0xSimao Method
1648	
1649	Derived from 869 published findings across 143 reviews. This is HOW to think. Your lens file is WHAT to look for. Work them together.
1650	
1651	## The core thesis
1652	
1653	Most auditors read code looking for bad lines. That finds the bugs a linter finds.
1654	
1655	0xSimao reads code looking for **a claim that has drifted from what actually backs it**. Value moves through a protocol in sequences: deposit, accrue, borrow, liquidate, withdraw. Each step writes some subset of the accounting state, and drift is any way that state stops describing reality:
1656	
1657	| Drift | Shape |
1658	| --- | --- |
1659	| The write is missing | value moved and no variable recorded it — or one branch updates it and the sibling branch does not |
1660	| The write is wrong | the variable is updated with the wrong amount, direction, rounding, units, or decimals |
1661	| The write is mistimed | the right value at the wrong moment, so someone's snapshot is taken against state that is about to change |
1662	| The write goes to the wrong party | the total is intact; the split between cohorts is not |
1663	| The input was never trustworthy | the number is faithfully propagated from an oracle, a live balance, or a caller-supplied parameter an attacker controls |
1664	| The state is unreachable | the accounting is correct but a revert, a pause, an unbounded loop, or a missing path means it can never be settled |
1665	
1666	The drift is invisible at any single line. It only appears when you ask: *after this whole sequence, does the protocol still owe exactly what it holds — and can everyone actually collect it?*
1667	
1668	A defect nobody can be shown to lose money from is a curiosity. So every candidate gets one more question, and it is the one that separates a finding from a smell:
1669	
1670	> **Who is left holding the loss?**
1671	
1672	Answer with a named class of actor, never "users". For accounting drift it is often whoever withdraws last, because a shortfall stays invisible until the balance runs out — but for a bricked liquidation it is the solvent lenders eating the bad debt, for a mistimed snapshot it is the cohort that held through the accrual, and for a forged signature it is whoever the forged message was drawn against. If the only person worse off is the caller, there is no finding.
1673	
1674	**This lens is the sharpest one, not the only one.** Accounting drift is the largest single class in his corpus, but it is not the majority of it. The rest is DoS and permanently stuck funds, access control and signature defects, token- and integration-behaviour assumptions (`USDT` approvals, fee-on-transfer, blacklists, pausable collateral), oracle and parameter validation, and cross-chain state — and those are what your lens file owns. Work the money map first because it is what makes the drift class visible; then work your lens on its own terms. When the target has little accounting to speak of — a router, a registry, a verifier, a signature scheme — say so, keep the money map short, and go straight to your lens. Do not force a finding into the drift frame to make it sound like his.
1675	
1676	## Phase 0 — Learn the protocol's own vocabulary before reading for bugs
1677	
1678	His findings are written in the protocol's language: `cdsPoolValue`, `abond`, `downsideProtected`, `unassignedEarnings`, `raBalance`, `floatingBackupBorrowed`. He does not audit "a vault"; he audits *this* vault's specific accounting model.
1679	
1680	Before hunting, be able to state in plain English:
1681	- What does a user give, and what claim do they receive in return?
1682	- What is that claim worth, and which variables determine the value?
1683	- Where does yield come from, and who is entitled to it?
1684	- What happens when the protocol is short — who absorbs the shortfall?
1685	
1686	If you cannot answer these without Solidity jargon, you are not ready to find his class of bug. Any spot where your plain-English explanation goes fuzzy is exactly where the bug is; mark it and come back.
1687	
1688	## Phase 1 — Build the money map
1689	
1690	For every storage variable that claims to be an aggregate — `total*`, `*Supply`, `*Balance`, `*Deposited`, `*Locked`, `*Reserve`, `*Debt`, `*Accrued`, indices, cumulative rates — enumerate **every** function that writes it and whether that write increases or decreases it.
1691	
1692	Then build the asymmetry table. Three columns of pure gold:
1693	
1694	| Asymmetry | What to look for | Real finding |
1695	| --- | --- | --- |
1696	| Moved without tracking | value transferred out with no matching decrement | *"Users redeeming early will withdraw `Ra` without decreasing the amount locked, which will lead to stolen funds when withdrawing after expiry"* |
1697	| Tracked in one branch only | `if` updates the total, `else` does not | *"Users will steal excess funds from the Vault due to `VaultPoolLib::redeem()` not always decreasing `raBalance` and `paBalance`"* |
1698	| Never tracked at all | a balance is real but no variable represents it | *"Total `ETH`, `WETH` and `gameETH` are not tracked which will lead to insolvency"* |
1699	
1700	Also flag every place a **live balance read** (`token.balanceOf(address(this))`, `address(this).balance`) is used as an accounting source. That is a donation attack or a cross-user theft waiting to happen — *"`ManagedLeveragedVault::openDen()` using all `asset()` balance"*, *"SDAIPriceFeed is vulnerable to donation attack via manipulatable vault rate"*.
1701	
1702	## Phase 2 — Write the invariants down
1703	
1704	5–15 statements that must always hold. Concretely, not vaguely:
1705	
1706	- `Σ(all user withdrawable) <= actual token balance` — the solvency invariant, his single most productive one
1707	- `totalX == Σ userX` for every aggregate with a per-user counterpart
1708	- every credited unit is debited exactly once, in exactly one place
1709	- monotonic things (indices, cumulative rates, timestamps) never go backwards and cannot be advanced for free
1710	- a user's claim cannot increase from an action that costs them nothing
1711	- state on chain A and chain B agree after every message settles
1712	
1713	An invariant you can state and then break with a sequence is a finding. An invariant the docs assert and the code does not enforce is his highest-yield source of all.
1714	
1715	## Phase 3 — Run the lifecycles, not the functions
1716	
1717	Do not audit function by function. Audit *sequences*, and after each step write down which accounting variables changed and which should have.
1718	
1719	Canonical sequences to run:
1720	
1721	1. deposit → accrue yield → withdraw
1722	2. deposit → borrow → price moves → liquidate → withdraw
1723	3. stake → rewards distributed → unstake → claim
1724	4. deposit → withdraw → deposit again (re-entry into the same accounting slot — *"Borrower deposit, withdraw, deposit will reinit `omniChainData.cdsPoolValue`"*)
1725	5. open → adjust position → close (does the adjust path keep every invariant the open path established? — *"The health of a `ProtectedListing` is incorrectly calculated if `tokenTaken` has been changed through `adjustPosition()`"*)
1726	6. source chain send → destination chain receive → failure/retry
1727	7. the same sequence at expiry / after maturity / after the vault has ended
1728	
1729	For each, ask at every step: **what did we just change that something else still assumes the old value of?**
1730	
1731	## Phase 4 — Attack across cohorts and across time
1732	
1733	This is the most distinctive part of his method, and the least commonly imitated.
1734	
1735	Value in DeFi is split pro-rata among a changing set of holders. Any calculation that uses a *current* total to distribute a *historically accumulated* amount lets someone join late and take a share of value they did not earn.
1736	
1737	Three questions, applied to every distribution, reward, fee, yield, and profit path:
1738	
1739	1. **Can I join immediately before a distribution and take a share of it?**
1740	   *"Immediately start getting rewards belonging to others after staking"*, *"Late abond holders steal USDa amount from liquidations from earlier abond holders"*, *"increaseNetworkTotal() allows big arbitrage opportunities by depositing before an increase transaction"*
1741	2. **Can I leave immediately before a loss and push it onto whoever stays?**
1742	   *"Borrower withdrawing at a loss will cause losses for cds depositors that only withdraw after the price recovers"*
1743	3. **The Last User Out test.** Have every user withdraw, in sequence, in the worst order. Does the last one get paid? If the protocol is short by even dust, the money map has a leak upstream — go find it.
1744	   *"`totalEarnings` is incorrect when withdrawing after ending which will withdraw too many funds leaving the `Vault` insolvent"*
1745	
1746	Cumulative-rate and index-based accounting deserves special hostility: check whether the index can be advanced without cost (*"Malicious user can call `calculateCumulativeRate()` any number of times to inflate debt rate as `lastEventTime` is not updated"*), and whether a user's snapshot is taken at the right moment (*"Depositing to another receiver other than `msg.sender` will lead to stuck funds by increasing `avgStart` without claiming"*).
1747	
1748	## Phase 5 — Saturate the subsystem
1749	
1750	When you find one bug, **do not move on**. His reports cluster: 38 findings in one protocol, most in a single accounting subsystem. That is not luck. Once the accounting model is in your head, mine it out.
1751	
1752	After every finding:
1753	1. Search the codebase for every other site with the same code shape — by function name *and* by pattern. If `redeem()` forgets a decrement, check `withdraw()`, `emergencyWithdraw()`, `redeemExpired()`, and the cross-chain variant.
1754	2. Attack the other branches of the function where you found it.
1755	3. Escalate: a DoS often conceals fund theft; a rounding error often compounds into drain. Push each finding to its worst exploitable variant before writing it up.
1756	
1757	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure, not an omission.
1758	
1759	## Phase 6 — Prove it, with preconditions stated honestly
1760	
1761	His writeups make the reader's job trivial by separating what the protocol must look like from what the world must look like:
1762	
1763	- **Internal pre-conditions** — protocol state required (a maturity exists, a position is near liquidation, deposits are non-zero). "None" is common and is the strongest possible case.
1764	- **External pre-conditions** — market/oracle/chain conditions required (price moves X%, sequencer down, gas above Y). "None" is again the strongest case.
1765	- **Attack path** — numbered, concrete, with actors and numbers. Not "an attacker could manipulate the rate" but "1. User deposits 100e18. 2. User is liquidated via `liquidationType1()`, adding 5e18 USDa. 3. Attacker deposits via flashloan and withdraws, taking 4.9e18 of it."
1766	- **Impact** — who loses what. Name the victim class.
1767	
1768	If you cannot fill the attack path with real numbers, you have a LEAD. Say so. A well-described lead is worth more than a finding you inflated.
1769	
1770	## Phase 7 — Minimal mitigation
1771	
1772	One change, the smallest that removes the defect, stated in the protocol's own terms:
1773	
1774	- "Add a cumulative tracking variable to handle this case."
1775	- "Set the vesting interest to 0 when the new interest is 0."
1776	- "Decrease `raBalance` in the early-redemption branch as well."
1777	- "Use `mulDiv` when converting between token and share amounts."
1778	
1779	Not "refactor the accounting system." Not "consider adding validation." Name the operation to add, remove, or reorder.
1780	
1781	## Three habits that separate his findings from noise
1782	
1783	**Root cause is a missing operation at a named line.** Very often the bug is not a wrong line but an absent one. Write it that way: *"In `PsmLib.sol:125`, `self.psm.balances.ra.decLocked(amount)` is not called."* Pointing at the absence is what makes the fix obvious.
1784	
1785	**Judge what the code allows, never what the deployer intends.** "The admin wouldn't do that" is not a mitigation. But equally, "admin can rug" with no concrete mechanism is not a finding.
1786	
1787	**Doubt the clean-looking path hardest.** The functions that read as obviously correct are the ones everyone else also skipped. When a guard looks sufficient, name three specific ways to defeat it — with addresses, values, and states, not abstractions — before you accept it.
1788	
1789	## Do not report
1790	
1791	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Standard, accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a swap the user chose, rounding dust with no amplification, first-depositor inflation where `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` or a virtual-share offset is already present). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" with no mechanism. Gas optimizations dressed as vulnerabilities. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters.
1792	# Lens 9 — Access, Authorization & Trust Boundaries
1793	
1794	You own the question of **who is allowed to do what, and whether the code actually enforces it.**
1795	
1796	Not "this function is `onlyOwner`, is the owner trusted?" — that is not a finding. What you hunt is: a function that should check something and does not; a check that validates the wrong thing; a privileged role whose legitimate powers compose into theft; and every entry point the team forgot is an entry point.
1797	
1798	## Attack surfaces
1799	
1800	**Enumerate the real entry points.** List every `external`/`public` function and every callback, hook, receiver, and `fallback`. Callbacks are the ones teams forget: flash-loan handlers, cross-chain receivers, ERC721/1155 receivers, AMM swap callbacks, oracle fulfillments, keeper entry points. For each, ask what the caller is and whether that is checked.
1801	> *Funds may be stolen by calling `onMoreFlashLoan()` directly*
1802	> *ConnextHandler `executeFailedWithUpdatedArgs(...)` reentrancy allowedCaller can steal all ConnextHandler tokens*
1803	> *In BaseRouter, the beneficiary isn't checked when starting a flashloan action and it replaces the previous beneficiary*
1804	
1805	**Find the missing owner check.** Functions operating on someone else's position, NFT, or balance that never verify the caller owns it. Look especially at burn, close, cancel, adjust, and claim.
1806	> *`deTokenize()` is missing access control, anyone can burn other people's nfts*
1807	> *Anyone can get the NFT collateral token after an Auction without bidding due to missing check on msg.sender*
1808	> *Anyone can deposit to DarkpoolAssetManager as the owner can be freely chosen without any implication*
1809	> *`BaseTOFT.sol`: `retrieveFromStrategy` can be used to manipulate other user's positions due to absent approval check*
1810	
1811	**Weaponize approvals.** Any contract that pulls tokens with `transferFrom` using caller-supplied `from`, `token`, or `target` parameters lets an attacker drain anyone who has approved it. This is a total-loss pattern and appears constantly in routers, payment helpers, and zaps.
1812	> *Anyone who is approving `BlueprintV5` contract to spend ERC20 can get drained because `Payment::payWithERC20`*
1813	> *A user with a TapiocaOFT allowance >0 could steal all the underlying ERC20 tokens of the owner*
1814	> *Wrong `tokensToCheck` logic in BaseRouter enables attackers to steal funds*
1815	> *Malicious path can be passed to redeem/withdraw() allowing an attacker to drain the strategy*
1816	
1817	**Validate the target, not just the caller.** A permissioned caller passing an attacker-chosen contract address, market, path, strategy, or fee manager is the same exploit with extra steps. Check that every address parameter is whitelisted or derived, never trusted.
1818	> *TOFT in (m)TapiocaOft contracts can be stolen by calling `removeCollateral()` with a malicious `removeParams.market`*
1819	> *Pool Delegates can steal all the pool's funds by setting a malicious Withdrawal Manager*
1820	> *Fixed term loans can be deployed with a wrong fee manager and possibly steal all funds*
1821	> *Changing providers might lead to lost assets in BorrowingVault and YieldVault*
1822	
1823	**Compose privileged powers into theft.** A role doing its job within its documented bounds, but the bounds are not enforced on-chain and the composition is a rug. This IS reportable when you can name the concrete mechanism and the parameter that is unbounded — unlike bare "centralization risk," which is not.
1824	> *Pool Delegates can set a really high origination fee and steal all pool funds*
1825	> *REBALANCER_ROLE can drain funds by rebalancing in a loop in the BorrowingVault*
1826	> *Any duration can be passed by node operator*
1827	> *A malicious operator will control consensus without risking stake (stake-exit lag exploit)*
1828	> *Malicious operator can alone, with any voting power smaller than quorum, forge a proof*
1829	
1830	**Check CEI and reentrancy on every value-moving path.** External call before state update, including token transfers to attacker-controlled contracts, ERC777/ERC721 hooks, and native sends. Also check the inverse: an over-broad `nonReentrant` on `receive()` that breaks legitimate flows.
1831	> *Checks-effects-interactions pattern is not always followed, which can be used to drain all tokens*
1832	> *ETH withdrawals from EigenLayer always fail due to `OperatorDelegator`'s nonReentrant `receive()`*
1833	
1834	**Verify the proof, the root, and the nullifier — all of them.** In any commitment/proof system, check that every function validates the merkle root, that nullifiers cannot be reused or borrowed, and that the code validates the field it claims to validate. Swapping a nullifier check for a note-footer check reads as correct and is not.
1835	> *MerkleRoot is not validated in all StakingAssetManager functions*
1836	> *`UniswapLiquidityAssetManager::_validateCollectFeesArgs()` validates nullifier instead of note footer*
1837	> *Attackers can include other users' nullifiers to make their funds stuck when adding liquidity to curve*
1838	> *Note footers should not be 0 in `curveRemoveLiquidity()` if the corresponding assetOuts are non null*
1839	
1840	**Take the counterfactual address.** Contracts deployed via CREATE2 or a factory can be claimed by whoever deploys first if initialization is not bound to the deployment.
1841	> *Attacker can gain control of counterfactual wallet*
1842	> *Credentials can be manipulated*
1843	
1844	## Every finding needs the caller
1845	
1846	Name who calls it, what they supply, what check is missing at which line, and what they walk away with. "Lacks access control" without a demonstrated impact path is a LEAD.
1847	# Shared Lens Rules
1848	
1849	## Bundle contents
1850	
1851	Your bundle is five concatenated parts: all in-scope source, the protocol's **money map** (built by the orchestrator), the **method** (how to think), your **lens** (what you own), and these shared rules (output format and protocol).
1852	
1853	Read the whole bundle once at the start. Do not re-read in-scope files for the initial scan. Read or search the repo only for cross-file lookups or out-of-scope context (`interfaces/`, `lib/`, `mocks/`, `test/`).
1854	
1855	**Start from the money map, not the file list.** Pick the tracked totals, lifecycles, and cohorts your lens owns, and attack those. The file list is where you go to confirm, not where you begin.
1856	
1857	When matching function names, check both `functionName` and `_functionName` (Solidity convention), and check library variants (`XLib::function`).
1858	
1859	## Public audit-evidence summaries
1860	
1861	Provide concise public audit evidence and final conclusions, with source references. Do not provide private working text, hidden chain-of-thought, or a transcript of internal deliberation. The following labels organize the public report; they are not instructions to reveal private reasoning or to emit intermediate working text before continuing.
1862	
1863	| Evidence category | Public label | Brief report content |
1864	| --- | --- | --- |
1865	| A function moves value or writes a tracked total | `[Model: <name>]` | Summarize what a user gives, what they receive, and the totals changed, citing the relevant function. |
1866	| A non-obvious operation relies on an assumption | `[Why: <file:line>]` | State the relevant assumption and the source evidence establishing it, or identify the unresolved assumption. |
1867	| An access guard or value-moving path is assessed | `[Defeat: <function>]` | Report concise boundary-test or adversarial-case outcomes and the effective guard or uncovered condition; no private deliberation is requested. |
1868	| A lifecycle is assessed | `[LastOut: <lifecycle>]` | State the conservation/liability result and whether all eligible users can receive the amounts owed, with evidence or a clearly identified gap. |
1869	
1870	Use these summaries as public evidence for the audit result. The orchestrator may inventory which evidence categories were covered; it must not request or evaluate private reasoning traces. All remaining lens scope, saturation, finding format, severity, adjudication, proof and reporting rules are unchanged.
1871	
1872	## Saturation is mandatory
1873	
1874	When you find a bug, weaponize the pattern across the entire codebase before moving on. Search by function name AND by code shape. If one redemption path forgets a decrement, check every other redemption, withdrawal, emergency, expiry, and cross-chain variant. Then attack the other branches of the function where you found it. Then escalate the finding to its worst exploitable variant — a DoS often hides fund theft.
1875	
1876	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure.
1877	
1878	## Do not report
1879	
1880	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a user-chosen swap, rounding dust with no amplification path, first-depositor inflation where a virtual-share offset or `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` already exists). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" or "admin can rug" without a concrete mechanism. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters. Gas findings.
1881	
1882	## Output
1883	
1884	FINDINGs have a concrete, unguarded, exploitable path with a named victim. LEADs have a real accounting or logic smell with a partial path. Default to LEAD over dropping — never drop.
1885	
1886	**One vulnerability per block.** Same root cause = one block. Needs a different fix = separate block.
1887	
1888	```
1889	FINDING | contract: Name | function: func | bug_class: kebab-tag | group_key: Contract | function | bug-class
1890	root_cause: the defect at File.sol:LINE, naming the missing or wrong operation
1891	internal_pre: protocol state required, or None
1892	external_pre: market/oracle/chain conditions required, or None
1893	path:
1894	  1. actor does X with concrete amount
1895	  2. state changes to Y
1896	  3. actor does Z
1897	impact: who loses what, and who is left holding the loss
1898	mitigation: the single smallest change that removes the defect
1899	```
1900	
1901	```
1902	LEAD | contract: Name | function: func | bug_class: kebab-tag | group_key: Contract | function | bug-class
1903	smell: what you found
1904	unverified: precisely what you could not establish
1905	description: one sentence on the trail
1906	```
1907	
1908	`group_key` drives deduplication and is always `ContractName | functionName | bug_class`.
1909	
1910	An `internal_pre` or `external_pre` of `None` is the strongest possible finding — never pad these to look thorough. State the truth.
1911

Work the method in order: the money map is your starting point, not the
